HARVEST HELP FROM UNITED STATES. On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to ask the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) certain questions with regard to the regulations under which harvesting help may enter Canada, and, with the permission of the House, I will read a short extract from a letter, which shows the circumstances in the district south of Swift Current, where the entry 'offices are far apart: 1
1 live on the International line forty miles south of Admiral, and am familiar with conditions on both sides of the line. The last three years there have been hundreds cross at harvest and threshing time, but this year the report has spread that the regulations are so drastic that they are afraid to come into the country.
In view of this report, I would ask if the minister could not issue an announcement that bona fide harvesters will not be inteT-LMr. Macdonald.]
fered with, and that they need not travel to far distant points to get the necessary certificate.

Such an arrangement has been entered into between the Government of Canada and the Government at Washington. The deputy minister is working out the details. It is the intention of the Government to waive tire immigration regulations. Such an announcement will be made -in fact, it has already been made in the press.

Buffalo	 $41.00

CONSPICUOUS GALLANTRY Op A CANADIAN OFFICER.
On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I desire to refer to the case of a Canadian officer who has been honoured on three different occasions for distinguished conduct at the front. The record of one person being awarded these three distinctions is most unusual. In a supplement to the London Gazette, dated August 11, is

contained the approval of His Majesty the King for the award of the Victoria Cross to Captain William Avery Bishop, whose father resides at Owen Sound, Ontario. Captain Bishop belongs to the Canadian Cavalry, and was attached to the Royal Flying Corps. He already possesses the Distinguished Service Order and the Military Cross. Reference has already been made to the matter in the press, but I thought it desirable to convey the facts to the House in order that a record of them may be placed on Hansard. The paragraph in the London Gazette reads as follows:
The award was made for most conspicuous bravery, determination and skill. Bishop, working independently, flew first to an enemy aerodrome. Finding no machine about, he flew to another aerodrome about three miles southeast, and at least twelve miles behind the German line. Seven machines, some with engines running, were on the ground there. He attacked these from about fifty feet up, and a mechanic who was starting an engine was seen to fall. One enemy aeroplane got off the ground but from a height of sixty feet Bishop fired fifteen rounds at very close range and it crashed to the ground. A second machine got off the ground ; Bishop fired thirty rounds at one hundred and fifty yards' range and it fell into a tree. Two more machines then rose. One he engaged at a height of one thousand feet. The enemy machine crashed to the ground three hundred yards from the aerodrome. Afterwards Bishop emptied the whole drum from his machine gun into a fourth enemy aeroplane and then returned to his station. Four hostile scouts were about one thousand feet above him for about a mile on the return journey, but would not attack. Bishop s machine was very badly shot about by mach ne gun fire from the ground.

Yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) intimated that to-day he would make a statement with regard to the supply of Pennsylvania coal in the West.

I do not know
that I can say'anything very definite about it. The facts which are apparent are these. First, there is a great and unprecedented call for coal in the United States. Second, both water and railway carriage are inadequate for the quick supply of coal, and that reacts upon the output of the mines. That applies particularly to the eastern and middle portions of the United States. As regards the lakes, the chief difficulty has been and is the matter of railroad transport from the mines to lake ports. Lack of means of transport has had the effect of causing several, perhaps many, grain and ore vessels Ito come 'back to the north with water ballast rather than with coal. Everything that can be done by the United States authorities and by the Fuel Controller is being done to co-ordinate the transport facilities and to hasten the delivery of coal. As to what will be accomplished, I cannot' speak definitely at present.
Will the minister kindly tell us what is being done? The condition that he speaks of with regard to transportation is well known.

that I can tell my hon. friend what is being done; that would take a long time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I think it was signed by the three Government directors only. Certain information was asked for last evening, which I am endeavouring to obtain, but which I am not yet in a position to give to the committee. As this information was asked for in connection with section 1, my suggestion is that that sec-
tion be allowed to stand and that we take up sections 2, 3 and 4 with a view to seeing whether we can make some progress with one or more of them.
I desire to give notice of some amendments with Tespect to clauses 2, 3 and 4, and in connection with those amendments I desire to make a few observations to the committee. It has been drawn to my attention by members of the House that section 3 gives the Governor in Council very wide powers indeed as to paying out money, issuing securities and giving guarantees. I wish to explain to the committee why that wide discretion was considered necessary in. connection with this measure. It is possible to estimate with a reasonable degree of accuracy the shortage which would require to be made up to meet underlying interest indebtedness incurred and to be incurred and for betterments and the purchase of rolling stock. But it is not possible to estimate what amount of money will be required to meet maturing shortterm obligations. I explained to the House that a number of short-term obligations of the Canadian Northern Railway company would mature from time to time during this and next year. I expressed the hope that the Canadian Northern Railway company would be able to meet those obligations by renewing them or making fresh issues from the proceeds of which they would be paid. However, on account of war conditions it is not certain that they will be able to do that; therefore it was considered advisable that the Dominion Government should take this power, this wide discretion, in order to be in a position to take care not only of underlying interest charges that the net earnings were not sufficient to meet needed betterments and equipment payments, but also one or more, possibly, of these short-term obligations, if it should chance that the Canadian Northern Railway company should' not be able to provide the necessary funds to meet them as they matured. The result is that this clause was drafted, which is very wide in its terms; indeed., when. I was -considering it I thought that it was too wide in its terms. I believe that so far as possible Parliament should be acquainted with the objects for which expenditures are made; in other words, that wherever possible there should be an estimate. I have accordingly drafted an amendment to section 3, of which I now desire to give notice. Before reading the amendment I would call the attention of the committee to the concluding portion of subsection 1 of section 3, which states that the Governor in Council may guaran-

tee payment in whole or in part and may give the obligations or securities of the Government in connection therewith.
The object of that was that the Government, instead of paying cash, might give its securities, and it might be able to guarantee a debt and in that way continue the obligation without immediate payment. But on thinking the matter over, I have reached the conclusion that I would rather he without those powers; that is, I would rather that the Dominion Government, instead of issuing securities in payment of obligations and instead of giving guarantees, to which of course there is a certain objection, should pay cash in connection with such financing as it has to do for this system. The amendment of which I purpose giving notice is this:
That all the words after "Fund" on line 4 page 2, of the Bill be struck out and the following substituted therefor:-
Provided however that until authorized by Parliament the total of such advances shall not exceed the sum of $25,000,000. A statement of any such advances showing in detail the purposes for which they were applied shall be presented to Parliament by the Minister of Finance within twenty days after the opening of the next ensuing session thereof.
As nearly as I can estimate, $25,000,000 ought until the next session to carry the system, including payments of obligations so far as we are able to estimate that they will fall due and cannot be renewed-and that is to some extent a matter of conjecture-and take care of all the interest payments and the payments for betterments and instalments upon rolling stock.
The hon. member for Calgary (Mr. E. B. Bennett), in his very interesting and able speech yesterday, referred to another matter which, I think is of some importance. He referred to the fact-and it is an undoubted fact-that the cost of labour and of material of all kinds is very much higher to-day owing to war conditions than it was in the period preceding the war or than it is likely to be in the period succeeding the war. The point he made was that the arbitrators might, in reaching a conclusion as to the value of this, stock, be guided, to some extent, by the reproduction cost of the physical assets of the Canadian Northern Railway company on a basis of war conditions. He thought it would be desirable that that should be obviated. Personally I would not be disposed to agree with the view that the arbitrators in valuing stock would, if they considered, in connection with such valuation, the reproduction cost of the physical assets of the system, regard the higher prices during war
conditions as governing that cost. The point was made yesterday by the Solicitor General that, if the Government were expropriating the physical assets of the Canadian Northern Railway company, possibly such a oouirse might be adopted. My own view is that, even in that case, it would not be adopted by a board of arbitrators, because it seems to me it would be manifestly wrong to take the inflated prices of material and equipment of every kind and the high cost of labour into account in reaching a conclusion as to the fair price to be paid for the physical properties of a railway company expropriated at a time like this. My opinion is not entitled to the weight of that of either the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) or the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). . In this connection, however, I would like to call attention to the view of Professor Swain, to which I referred the other day, as to the principles of valuation. Professor Swain at page 4 of his report emphasizes earning power as to the principal test of value, and I will quote him again for the information of the committee. He says:
There is no sentiment about a commercial property like a railroad. The real value of such a property is measured by its earning power and by nothing else. No matter how costly or how inexpensive it may have been originally, its value in exchange will be measured by its earning power. Prospective earning power, perhaps under altered conditions, must of course be considered. Some properties, therefore, have a so-called "strategic" value, because, while they may earn nothing by themselves, they may be combined with other properties in a way to produce or enhance earnings.
Then his statement, on the next page with regard to the valuation of physical assets is this:
Just what the present value, or the fair present value may be, is not easy to state, and probably cannot be stated. The courts, however, have frequently stated what it is not. They have again and again laid down the principle that it is not original cost. In some instances they have stated that it is not the cost of the reproduction new, but it is generally admitted, I think, that both the original cost and cost of reproduction new, and also the depreciation, depending upon circumstances, are all elements which may affect the judgment as to the "fair value."
He emphasizes earning power actual and potential, but in connection with a railway system such as this, my own view would be that if potential earnings were considered at all, it could be considered only as to the company in private hands as it is to-day, and in the serious financial

position in which it is. I stated that the other day. I would not admit for a moment that the prospective earning power of this system in the hands of a strong Government able to finance it should be considered by the arbitrators. On page 6, Professor Swain deals with this question which was Taised by the hon. member for Calgary and as to which I purpose giving notice to-day of an amendment. This is what Professor Swain says:
These principles were briefly discussed with your commission before the beginning- of the work. The problem, therefore to be performed by the force under my direction, was to ascertain the cost of reproduction new of the properties in question at the present time. By the phrase "at the present time" is not to be understood the present moment, in view of the inflated prices for materials and labour which have come about as a result of the war; but rather, the fair cost of reproduction new, assuming that the properties were to be reproduced at fair average prices prevailing during a brief period of years just before the war.
Professor Swain, therefore, in dealing with the question of reproduction cost in war time, clearly states that the inflated prices for material and labour are not to be taken into account, but rather that there should be considered the fair cost of reproduction "assuming "that the properties were to be reproduced at fair average prices prevailing during a brief period of years just before the war." I do not make his sentiments my own, because I do not think the matter is one on which I am called upon to express an opinion. But I desire to make the point ithat it is not probable that a board of arbitrators in fixing the value of the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company would be guided, in their deliberat-tions by the bearing which the high prices prevailing during the war have on the cost of reproduction. But after all is said and done, the question is a legal one, and one upon which I think no chances should be taken, and I therefore give notice that when we reach section 4 I shall move to add the following to subsection 2:
In determining the value of the said six hundred thousand shares the arbitrators, should they regard it as expedient to take into consideration the reproduction cost of the Canadian Northern Railway System, shall not include therein the increase in value, due to the war, of labour, materials, equipment or of any property.

The reason why those words were inserted was that the arbitrators might be able to proceed expeditiously in determining the value of the stock. But there does appear to be a doubt, so far as concerns an appeal to the Supreme Court, that if these words are left in, the court might find itself unable to review the award on the ground that the arbitrators had acted, not only as arbitrators, but as experts. I confess that I think it could be argued that to use their own judgment would mean using their own judgment having regard to the evidence. I am inclined, however, to the interpretation which has (been placed upon the words by the hon. member for Calgary and the hon. member for Pictou. I think it would be better that the words be left out, and I shall move accordingly:	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Then I misunderstood my hon. friend. I understood him to say yesterday that the Supreme Court had refused to set aside the award in a certain case because the arbitrators in the exercise of their own judgment had decided in a certain way. The principle that I thought was at stake was this: If arbitrators, in addition to being judges, so to speak, are made experts, so that they may act upon their own opinion in addition to considering evidence, the Court of Review might say, "How can we come to a different determination when it is open to these arbitrators to exercise their own judgment not only upon the evidence but with regard to tlje valuation"? stand, with a view to providing the information which has been asked for. I have been away for a day or two, but so far as I know we have not yet had complete information as to what we aTe going to acquire by this Bill. We acquire the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway company, ,and in that way we take over the whole system. The Canadian Northern Railway system is a very extended one, covering all the provinces of the Dominion -not entirely, but in some part-with the exception of one. If there was only one charter there would be no trouble. But, as my hon. friend is aware, the main charter controls quite a number of subsidiary charters. All these are to be acquired, and we do not know what they are. I think we should have a detailed statement of all the subsidiary charters controlled by the main charter. For instance, there are charters in Nova Scotia which are covered by this main chanter. There is also a very important question as to whether we acquire the Montreal terminals under this present Bill, and whether we acquire the Model City, which is an adjunct of the Canadian Northern Railway -company in Montreal. I would suggest to my hon. friend that before we take up section 1 we -should have a detailed statement of the different charters which will be covered by the Act now -proposed.

speechtext: Would my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) tell me what lease he is referring to?

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
A lease by the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company to the railway company for
4 p.m. the use of its facilities. The method adopted was the usual one adopted under circumstances of this kind. You create a company with power to issue securities and the securities have to be guaranteed by the rentals to be paid for the use of the terminals. In this case the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company, which owns the terminal facilities in Montreal, leases them to the Canadian Northern, but in order to give the securities any value they had to have behind them something more than the physical property of the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company. Therefore they leased the terminals at a rental to the Canadian Northern Railway system, including the Canadian Northern Quebec, and the rental is equivalent to the annual interest charges upon the securities. That has been assigned to trustees for the purpose of enabling the securities to be sold, but they have behind them something more than the mere physical property upon which they were issued.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Is that lease contained in any of the papers which have been brought down?

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
That lease was set forth in the statute passed by Parliament in 1916. We had it before us, and we considered it in the Railway Committee. The lease itself is set forth in the schedule to the Act. In so far as the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company is concerned, the position would be that the Canadian Northern Railway and the Canadian Northern Quebec have rented the terminals for an annual rental equivalent to



interest charges upon the securities. The Model City and the Port Mann terminals, which I apprehend are what are referred to by trie leader of the Opposition, are in no sense the property of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. They illustrate the second point I complained of yesterday, namely, the exploitation of subsidiary companies by these gentlemen to create inflated values, 'resulting in loss to small speculators. For instance there was $1,000,000 lost by one group of speculators through the Port Mann enterprise alone. But, we do not get that. A subdivision was made and the land was sold but	not	a (single share of	the
capital stock of the Model City, the Port Mann terminals, the fishery, or timber, of any of these companies come to us. That is my understanding of it as a result of the best consideration I have b&en able to give the matter from a perusal of the various documents in the statute-books, and I have no further information with regard to it. The Minister of Finance proposes to offer an amendment to one of the sections. But that amendment is not ample for the purpose of safeguarding the public interest. What we should say in the statute is that the question to he referred is: What is the present cash value per share of the outstanding shares of the capital stock of the Canadian Northern Railway Company? What we are endeavouring to fix is the value that appertains to the shares as shares and not the value that appertains to the $60,000,000 that would carry control. That is best illustrated by the experience in connection with the Northern Pacific. Members of this House who have been reading the life of the late Mr. J. J. Hill will (recall that Mr. Harriman attempted to get control of the Northern Pacific on the open market and that he nearly had control. It is interesting to remember that he would have secured control of the company if he had been able to secure the holdings of the two Scotch Canadians. That stock was bid up to $1,000 a share. That did not represent the intrinsic value of the shares, that was not the real value that attached to them; it was only the value that attached to them because possession of them carried with it the ability to control the corporation. Shares amounting to $60,000,000 carry with them control of the Canadian Northern system and it must be remembered that, control always has a market value. Whether it be a small or a big corporation, v control has its value. Whoever has con-
trol in this case can elect the directors and thereby control the operation of 9,500 miles of track, with all the subsidiary enterprises and at the same time control $40,000,000 cash during the year. Another illustration of the value of control is given by the Equitable Life Insurance Company. The Equitable Life is perhaps one of the greatest of our American financial institutions; yet it only has a capital stock of $100,000 and its dividends are limited to seven per cent per annum. The outstanding insurance is computed in the billions and its revenues in the hundreds of millions. General Dupont, since this war began, gave $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 to get control of the $100,000 of stock. These particular illustrations I submit, would warrant this House in inserting in this section adequate language to provide that what we pay Mackenzie and Mann for the equity of redemption; that is, the value of their shares, is not for control but for the value of $60,000,000 of shares in relation to the capital (Stock of $100,000,000. What the arbitration has to determine is the value of the outstanding shares.
The conclusion after that is a problem in multiplication-simply multiply the number of shares by the value fixed by the arbitrators.
With reference to the expression "their own judgment,?' my hon. friend from Pic-tou (Mr. Macdonald) did not follow me, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) could not have read what I have stated in Hansard-and I do not blame him for that. I was pointing out that it was desirable the words remain there. The expression "their own judgment" should be retained as, in the event of the acquisition of shares, you could not view them as you could a parcel of property. In the acquisition of a piece of property by expropriation, you can view the premises, and I desire to apply the principle here so that if the arbitrators travelled over the property of the railway company and saw its physical condition in arriving at the value of the shares, they would, in the exercise of "their own judgment," come within the provisions of the McKinnon case, and thereby enable the citizens of the country to have the benefit of the evidence, and the exercise of the judgment of the arbitrators in fixing the price to be paid for the shares of the company if such price is to be determined by reference to the value of the assets.

The Supreme Court of Canada said it would set aside the judgment of the Supreme Court of Alberta and sustain the award, not because there was no appeal, or that it was an improper case in which to appeal, but because the fact that the arbitrators did exercise their own judgment did not in any sense destroy the validity of the award or limit the right of appeal.

The Supreme Court would have before them the evidence, but there would be another element which they would not have before them; that is, the facts on which the arbitrators' had exercised an expert judgment. It occurred to me that that was ithe point the hon. gentleman from Calgary was referring to. It still strikes me as a pretty important point with regard to the question of appeal. I did not understand the statement of the hon. gentleman from Calgary as to the Supreme Court in the McKinnon case refusing to disallow the award. Minister of Finance ae to the effect of those words which it is proposed to strike out, and I think my hon. friend from Calgary in his argument yesterday was endeavouring to point out the danger that would ensue from these words being left -in, so far as the effect on an appeal court is concerned. Because, manifestly, the Board of Arbitrators would arrive at a conclusion not merely upon the evi-" denee submitted to them but by the exercise of their own judgment. They might take an expert view of the situation not based upon the evidence, and might arrive at the amount of the award in that way. You can well understand how the appellate

tribunal would say: It is impossible for us to enter into the question whether or not the best judgment of the arbitrators, exercised 'beyond the evidence, was a matter in which they erred. The argument of my hon. friend from Calgary, I think, requires most careful deliberation before coming to a conclusion, and perhaps it would be well that the consideration of this question should standi over until the minister has brought down the information which he intimated he intended to bring with reference to section 1. That is the section which provides for the taking over of the stock and is the vital section of the Bill-the whole principle of the measure is contained in section 1. The data as to who are the holders of the stock which is to be taken over is so material that the consideration of the whole measure turns upon that to a very great degree, and I should like the minister, in that connection, to intimate what information he can give us with reference to the $25,000,000 of convertible stock. Does he expect to be able, to give us any information which would indicate that a number of the stockholders were likely to come in and avail themselves of an award which fixed the value of the stock at a very high figure, and would enable them to get more than par for it? It is impossible for us to predicate in any way what award this tribunal might give, in fixing the value of the stock. Any one who has had any experience with reference to valuations or testing the question of value in the courts knows the tremendous number of matters that can be taken into consideration, more particularly in the case of an enterprise of the extent and possibilities of the Canadian Northern. So that I think we should have some information about the liability that is likely to arise, in addition to the nominal registered holdings of $100,000,000. We should understand the facts with regard to this extra $25,000,000, which, under the law, the holders could convert into common stock, for, if that is done, we shall be dealing, not with $100,000,000 of common stock of the company, but possibly with $125,000,000.

Why do we not confine ourselves to 51 per cent? To me it is perfectly obvious that the Dominion Government, while buying this stock, should buy all of it. They do not want a majority of the stock, with a minority stock to deal with. Their proper course is to buy all the stock.

speechtext:
I agree that we should acquire every dollar of the stock, but I do not agree that we should be subject to the chance of the holders of $25,000,000 worth of minority shares coming in and owning one-fifth of this road after we have put our money into it. That right should not be standing there. After we have put from $25,000,000 to $50,000,000 into it, certain men over in England will say: This is a good thing for us! just now there is no income in this company; I paid a big price for these income certificates; I can get no money out of them-and I would -much rather be a partner with the Dominion of Canada than have an outstanding

obligation with the Canadian Northern. What they will do is to exchange these income certificates for common stock; then we shall (find ourselves unable to deal with this enterprise as we please, in view of the holding overseas or somewhere else of this $25,000,000 worth of minority shares.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Does the income stock not pay dividends?

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Of course not;
the income certificates do not pay any dividend. They are five per cent income certificates, and they pay a dividend only when the surplus over the fixed charges is available for dividend purposes. They are just what their name indicates; an income certificate is a certificate the income of which is chargeable against surplus income after paying all fixed charges. -Therefore, unless there is a surplus aftej paying all fixed charges, there is no dividend on the income certificates. As a matter of fact, the income certificates that are outstanding were issued with respect to a special portion of the property. I understand that complaints have been made by the holders of the income certificates in England that upon the property on which these were originally charged there was a surplus available for dividends, because the Canadian Northern prairie section is a very profitable section. Theirr contention was that what they had was an income certificate against income in respect of that property, not in respect of the losing sections of the line in British Columbia and in eastern Canada. They have not established that point to the satisfaction of anybody, but I know that they have made that claim. It is not divulging any confidence to bring this to the attention of the committee, because these certificates can be bought on the open market. Some investors in England paid $106 for $100 par value of these certificates. The Canadian Northern received, I think, $25,000,000 net, after paying commissions. What the Solicitor-General (Mr. Meighen) said yesterday is sound: this Parliament extended the time for conversion by statute in the Act of 1914 until January 1, 1919. Section 12 of the Act reads as follows:
The capital stock of the Canadian Northern is hereby fixed at the sum of one hundred million dollars subject to increase only by the Parliament of Canada:
Provided that for the purpose of exchange of Income Charge Convertible Debenture Stock, secured by trust deed made to the British Empire Trust Company, Limited, and the National Trust Company, limited, dated 6th

May, 1910, not exceeding- twenty-five million dollars in all, there may, during the period of the option of exchange given by said Trust Deed to the holders of said debenture stock, viz., the years from January 1,	1916, to
January 1, 1919, inclusive, and during any extension of that period, be issued to such holders who may exercise said option, such amounts of capital stock, over and above one hundred million dollars as may be required for the purposes of such exchange, not exceeding one hundred dollars ($100) of capital stock for one hundred dollars ($100) of debenture stock and not exceeding in all twenty-five million dollap'rovided that the Canadian (Northern may extend the period of said option from time to time. The said additional twenty-five million dollars of capital stock is hereby authorized and shall be set apart for the sole purpose of such exchange and any fully paid stock deposited with the trustees of said trust deed for such purposes may be returned to the depositors
thereof:	.	,	. ,
Provided, also, -that no further issue of said Income Charge Convertible Debenture Stock shall be made under said trust deed.
As these income certificates are on the open market, something should be done to prevent, say, John Smith from going to the London Stock Exchange, buying $1,000 worth of these income certificates and becoming a partner with the Dominion of Canada in the ownership of the Canadian Northern. That is my case. '
. Mr. MEIGHEN: There was considerable discussion about these bonds in 1914. To understand the position it is necessary to make amply clear the nature of the bonds.
I do not know what it is secured on; my own understanding w.as that it was secured on the Canadian Northern Railway -Company's properties of every kind; that is to say, the properties of the parent company alone. The issue -was otf this nature: the Canadian Northern Railway Company made the issue, secured on their own property, and there were two exceptional provisions in the trust deed which secured the issue. One was that the debentures were to be entitled to dividends only out of profits over and: above previous fixed -charges -and operating expenses. Where there were no profits there was no accumulation, and they could not exact a dividend out of one year's profits by reason of a failure to pay dividend -before. That was the first exceptional provision. The other exceptional provision was this: the holders of these debentures were entitled to exchange debentures for stock-$100 debenture for $100 stock-at any time between the dates specified in the Act, January 1, 1916, and January 1, 1919.

Consequently, as there is no reasonable prospect of any exchange, and inasmuch as we should not take away the assets of people without making provision for the valuation of those assets, I do not think we should take action now. Suppose the worst

came to the worst; suppose those people in England, and those'citizens of Canada, of whom there is probably a greater number of them in England, who hold this debenture stock, should immediately come to the conclusion that under the efficient management of this Government that stock will immediately reach a value over par and consequently be worth more than the debentures, some of them who came to that conclusion might exchange. It would then be open to us to provide a similar measure to this and submit that stock which they exchanged to a court of arbitration for the determination of its value, and then we could take it. We would not be at any great loss because for every $100 worth of stock we then expropriated, we would get rid otf $100 of debt-$100 of debt would be exchanged for $100 worth of stock, and we would get the stock. Consequently, the debt would be gone, so that we would have nothing very great to fear.
In the first place, then, there is no reasonable possibility of any o.f those debentures being exchanged. Secondly, if there is, it is difficult to arrive at any just or practicable way of extinguishing that right of exchange. Thirdly, without extinguishing that right, we are in no peril whatever. While we do not wish to be partners with any one in this property-and the hon. member for Calgary is right when he states that we should own it out and out-we have a very fair method of extinguishing the interest of any partner who might possibly come in under this legislation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
'No, because this Bill
provides only for buying 600,000 shares.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: It would be wise to postpone this discussion unitil we get the necessary information. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) last night asked for certain information in particular as to who were the present holders of this stock, and if I understood the Minister of Finance aright, he promised to get that information. As yet, however, we have not received it, and there is other information to which we are entitled. Evidently, the Government brought down this measure without being equipped with the necessary information that the people of this country and we, as their representatives, are entitled to have. We are entitled to information concerning a thousand and one things-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Leave out the one.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
-but the information has not yet been furnished. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) last night referred to a disputed account. A contractor had made a deposit of some $18,000, of which $5,000 had been refunded, there [DOT]being still outstanding $13,000 which the contractor claims, but which claim the Canadian Northern do not recognize. In addition to that the contractor claimed the
balance of some $18,000 making a disputed account outstanding amounting to about $31,000 that evidently the Canadian Northern do not acknowledge. If we are to take over the stock of this road and become the owners, taking the place of Mackenzie and Mann as regards the financing of the road, it is well we should know how many of those outstanding accounts are floating around and not acknowledged or settled. We should know many things in connection with this transaction before we pass it through this House. There is, for instance, the question of the basis on which the arbitrators will determine as to the value of this stock.
The hon. member for Calgary suggested two bases:	First, the actual cost of the
Toad less depreciation, and secondly, what it would cost to reproduce the same property under present conditions. If the latter is adopted, no one can say what we should have to pay, because the cost of labour and material used in every kind of railway construction has increased in very great degree. The gate is left open, the arbitrators can adopt whichever course they see fit. I think the safer and wiser way would be to deal with the stock from the point of view of what assistance it had been in the construction of the road. I notice that the commissioners say in their report that there is no money to be derived from the sale of the stock which was used in the construction of the road. If that be true, and I do not think there is any doubt about it, what need is there to arbitrate to find out the value when the stock has no value?
The hon. member for Calgary also told us yesterday that prior to the legislation of 1914 the capital stock of the company was $70,000,000, but then, by a simple stroke of the legislative pen, we created $25,000,000 more stock, which represented no actual value. To-day, we are asked to place a value on that $25,000,000 of stock by arbitration.
I think it would hasten the passage of this Bill if we adjourned the debate and proceeded with some other business until we get the necessary information. I have never been disposed to delay the proceedings of this House, but I certainly am not disposed to allowing this legislation to go through, if I can help it, until we are	given full information,	and I
trust that members on both sides of the House who are interested in the welfare of the country will support me in that suggestion. It will be a bad enough bar-

gain when we have all the facta before us, but in a matter of this magnitude, involving the expenditure of $600,000,000 we should at least know how bad a bargain we are making, and should not pass this legislation in any light or hasty manner. I repeat that the Government have not shown a disposition to give the House the information to which it is entitled, and I again urge the Minister of Finance to adjourn this debate and proceed with some other business, because I think by .so doing he will make just as quick progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend has not read Hansard in so far as it records this debate, nor the documents which have been already filed. I think it would be impossible in a transaction of this magnitude to give the uttermost details in connection with minor claims such as my hon. friend has referred to. The hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) brought up the question of claims last night, and I gave a full explanation with regard to the particular claim he referred to. It is a claim that is not admitted; it is contested. My hon. friend would not contend that the Department of Railways should insist upon the payment of a contested claim without investigation. The Department of Railways have investigated this particular claim, and have suggested a mode of solution which appears to them, and appears to me, to be reasonable, but which has not been availed of by the parties who have complained about the matter. Not only that, but there is ample money in the way of drawback in the Department of Railways to take care of that claim. All that was stated last evening.
As far as the stock is concerned, I stated that I would endeavour to get the information for the House, and I am doing so. When, my hon. friend says that the Government has come down to the House without adequate information, so far as the purchase of stock is concerned, for carrying out this transaction, I do not agree with him. For this reason: The Dominion Government owns 40 per cent of the fully paid up stock of this road. We provide in the agreement for the acquisition of the remaining 600,000 shares. We know where we can get five-sixths of the shares. We know that 51 per cent, which is more than five-sixths of the 600,000 shares other than those held by the Dominion Government, will come in. That leaves only 9 per cent of shares. If the 9 per cent come in they will be dealt with under the agreement.

If they do not come in, there is power in the Bill enabling the Government to declare that they are vested in His Majesty, and their owners will be entitled to the ' price which the others receive.
So far as the Government's programme before the House is concerned, for providing the machinery to take over the remaining capital stock of the Canadian Northern railway, it is complete. All the inforinm-tion as to the general financial position of the company is already before the House in the blue books which have been published and in the statements which have been laid upon the Table. More than that, the House is generally familiar with the Canadian Northern Railway situation, which has been before the House for practically the last ten years. In 1914 a most thorough investigation was made by accountants and experts with a view to determining the facts. The sessional papers of that year are full of information respecting the Canadian Northern. We have the balance sheet certified by the auditors, and we have our own auditors carrying on a continuous audit. We have had Government directors on the board for the past year. While there may be a number of outstanding accounts, some of them" contested and others not, it seems to me that we have substantially before us the information which would enable the House, which is not a judicial body, to come to a conclusion such as Parliament comes to on a question of this kind. In all these large transactions, whether it is a question of building a transcontinental railway, or of affording assistance to the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Canadian Northern, while it is desirable to have all reasonable information, it is not possible to get down to the meticulous information that would cover every particular point. If, however, there is any information that is not before the House other than that which has been asked for, and which it is reasonable to ask for and possibly to get, I shall be disposed to use my best endeavours to obtain it for the House.
We might go on with the other sections until six o'clock, and take u,p some other Bill this evening. I thought possibly the Income T,ax Bill might be taken up, if the committee is -of opinion that we cannot make much progress with regard to section 1. The Prime Minister is not here, and I would prefer that hon. gentlemen would address themselves to section 2, with a view to seeing whether we cannot make some progress.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: There is a good deal of force in the remarks made foy my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea), that the information first supplied by the Government was rather scanty. I must say the Minister of Finance has been very courteous and ready to give any information asked for. I think the amendment which he has proposed had better wait until we come to discuss that section. In the meantime, I would ask for more information than we have received so far, upon some other points. I have asked information as to what we acquire, and my hon. friend has satisfied me that in acquiring the stock of the parent company what we acquire is limited to what is set forth in the schedule of 1914. So far, so good, and we understand where we are.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: The information I gave is brought down to date.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
Yes, I understand. As a point of law everything is detailed in the Act of 1914. We acquire what is stated in the schedule to the Act of 1914, nothing more and nothing less. A moment ago I mentioned The Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company, which is .a very important part of the terminals of the road. My hon. friend has not given us any information, so far -as I know, as to the liabilities, possibilities, and obligations we are assuming when we acquire this company. The Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company provides for the terminal of the road at Montreal. I do not know whether the tunnel has been completed or not, but I understand it is practically so. There is, however, a great deal still to be done in connection with the completion of the terminus at Montreal, .and we have had no estimate as to what it will cost to complete that portion and make it a working enterprise. At the present time the Canadian Northern has no terminus in the western section of Montreal. It has a temporary terminus in the east end of the city. Like the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian Northern must have two stations there, one in the east and one in the west. I do not know whether it is using the eastern station or not, but, in any event, it must have a western station, and there will be a great liability upon the Government to complete this. My hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) called attention yesterday to the terminal in British Columbia. He said: The Canadian Northern is the owner of Northern Pacific, stock. That will now belong to us. If you take the line from Vancouver
to the Kamloops valley, a large quantity of property has been acquired. As regards British Columbia we find that there is $4,725,945.51 in the banks, and the total liabilities with respect to western lines uncompleted is only $1,612,000, so that there must be in the banks of British Columbia a large sum of money arising from the sale of securities that has to be used for the construction of terminals and lines which we are bound to construct.
We have had no information whatever upon those lines which we are bound to construct in British Columbia. My hon. friend will realize that Parliament cannot be expected to pass this Bill until we have positive information on these points.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I think I gave the House the information my right hon. friend asks for, respecting the terminals.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: I did not see the figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
It is no trouble
giving them again. Three terminals have been referred to, the Montreal terminal, the Toronto terminal, and the Pacific Coast terminal. The estimated cost to complete those terminals is as follows: the Montreal terminal, 5578,000; the Toronto terminal, $388,094; the Pacific Coast terminal, $1,-500,000-a total of $2,466,094. Add to that the estimated cost to complete lines already under construction, as follows: western lines, $1,612,005, eastern lines, $110,000, a total of $1,722,005. This makes the estimate of the requirements for the construction, programme the Canadian Northern has now under way, $4,188,099. As provision to meet these payments, there is cash in trust accounts, representing the proceeds of bonds which have been sold, and applicable to the construction of these terminals, and those western lines $3,683,831-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: That is in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OP CANADIAN NORTHERN .RAILWAY BILL RESUMED IN COMMITTEE.
speechtext: Yes-government guaranteed securities $217,160, Canadian Northern four per cent debenture stock, $287,108, making a total of $4,188,097. With regard to the last item, Canadian Northern four per cent debenture stock, $287,108, my own opinion is that it is not readily saleable. The Comptroller of Railways is in close touch with the operations of the company, by reason of the guarantees and the subsidies which the Dominion Government has given in respect of their lines. He has checked these figures very carefully and there'seems no reason to doubt their accuracy. I shall get the other information for my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: What is meant by completing the programme of the Canadian Northern?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Probably I should has said, the programme actually under construction-not the ultimate programme.
Does it mean continuing every branch so that it -will no longer be a blind line, for example?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Only the work actually under construction; with the idea of determining what is the outstanding liability and what funds there are to meet it. Of course, in any railway system, as my hon. friend knows better than I do, because he is from the West, extensions will have to be made continually. The construction of those extensions will depend, first, upon the urgency of the need for them, and secondly, upon the financial situation. I have no doubt that the Canadian Northern Railway system, the Grand Trunk Pacific system, and even the Canadian Pacific have had extensions in contemplation on many lines, but the programme has been held up by reason of war conditions, and difficulty of financing.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The information my hon. friend gives is partly satisfactory, but it is not complete.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What else is
there?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
For instance, my hon. friend says it will cost $578,000 to complete the terminus in Montreal, if I caught the figures correctly. It is impossible that half a million dollars will complete the terminals in that city-the actual, present programme. But, as to what it will cost to complete the terminals in Montreal we have no information. A railway is always building, always spending money. The Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk, the New York Central, are always constructing and building, but these .railways are going concerns; they are railways in operation. The Canadian Northern, to a certain extent, is a going concern, but it is only partially so. It is not a going concern in Montreal to-day. The Canadian Northern is not completed to Montreal, and it is of the greatest importance, with reference to its own profit and the interests of the country, that it should be completed to Montreal. I am quite a believer in the Canadian Northern and I believe that when it is completed, as it was conceived by its promoters, from Edmonton to Montreal, it will have a very great future

before it. But it is to be completed and that is what we want the information about. My hon. friend has not told us .how many millions of dollars will be necessary to complete the entrance of the Canadian Northern to Montreal. He has information only in reference to the programme that they have in contemplation this year, or that they had, perhaps, three years ago, when they were interrupted by the war. But this programme is not complete and it must be considerably supplemented in order that the Canadian Northern, may become a going concern especially in the eastern part of Canada.
Sir THOMA'S WHITE: I am informed that the present construction programme is adequate to meet the needs of the system at this time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Do I understand that $500,000 or $600,000 will bring this Tailway to the terminals on Dorchester street?
'Sir THOMAS WHITE: The Comptroller of Railways informs me that that is so. I have no personal knowledge about it. The expenditure on terminals might be quite unlimited. Take Toronto, for example; for many years they have been getting on with a station wholly inadequate to the traffic requirements.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But there was a station.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was a
station. I understand there is to be a temporary station in connection with the Canadian Northern at Montreal, approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners. It is better to have a temporary station than not to have a station at all. But if we can look forward, as I think we can, to greatly increased business the time will come when this temporary station will not serve the purpose and when a proper station will be built. I do not think it is possible at this moment to .say 5 p.m. how many millions are to be spent on that terminal. Over a course of years, or in a generation, a great many millions might be spent on a terminal. The safeguard is that the company is not permitted to go beyond this programme.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend tells me that $570,000 will cover the expenditure on the terminals at Montreal. I understand that that expenditure will provide

a temporary station and enable trains to come to Dorchester street?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Comptroller
informs me that is absolutely correct.

Might I suggest to my
right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that he might be too'easily satisfied. I happen to know something about the Mount Royal terminal and station. While $570,000 may be sufficient to bring a train into the temporary station that, it is now stated, will be erected there, nothing at all is said about the enormous amount that will be paid by way of compensation and damages for land that has been taken and which has not yet been settled for. The claims have reached a huge sum. I happen to have personal knowledge of some of them, and I submit to the Minister of Finance that there should be placed before this committee, in addition to the information which has been asked for and which the minister has promised to bring down, a statement showing the actual amount determined so far to be paid and the undetermined claims that will have to be paid for land taken by the Mount Royal Tunnel and Terminal Company. The claims for land in and about the city of Montreal must run into a very large sum indeed. This committee should have the information before it is asked to put through the Bill. The request made for the postponement of the consideration of the Bill *was based on two grounds. It was based by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) upon the necessity of considering the amendments that have been proposed, and, secondly, by my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) upon a request for further information. In connection with the amendments might I suggest that if possible the amendments which were forecasted by the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett) might be submitted to the committee also, so that if there is any postponement of the discussion we shall have the benefit of having these amendments before us and we can consider them all. I would like to ask the hon. member for Calgary a question. Did I understand him to say that if the holders of the income certificates were to exercise their election within the time specified and the exchange for common stock were to take place, >sueh exchange would he made for a portion of the present $100,000,000 of stock.

No, I said that
any exchange would involve an increase in the capital stock beyond $100,000,000 and would introduce new shareholders into the enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall endeavour to get the information which my hon. friend requires in regard to the claims. I think the Comptroller of Railways can obtain it for him. iSome of the claims are in the courts. I am unable to say at the moment what the sum total will amount to. The fact that they are in the courts is not a reflection upon the company, because the claims may or may not be just. A portion of a bond issue was paid in connection with these charges in order to provide money for completion, and there is a balance on hand Which it is estimated will take care of the construction programme in immediate contemplation.

There is other information that I would like to have. The minister said that there was a specified sum of money available to complete the work which is called for by the programme. That amount must have been arrived at by some system of accounting or by a statement of some sort. I would like the minister to give us some information showing how that sum was arrived at and where geographically this programme is to be put into effect.
For example, in my riding there is a piece of the Canadian Northern railway which runs fifteen or twenty miles from the international boundary, and goes westward to Bengough, which is about straight south of a point between Regina and Moosejaw. But the line stops there quite suddenly and unexpectedly, although they have a portion of the supplies to continue the railway further. I am in doubt as to what the hon. minister calls building according to programme. This is at present a blind line, and it was never intended it should stop there. It was to serve the country west of that place, and that was the justification for building the railway, because people west were more urgently in need of the transportation. Does he mean that money now lies in the bank earmarked for that? Is it earmarked for the road beyond Bengough, or only up to Bengough? Because the road beyond Bengough was more essential to the people of that district than the road up to that point.
There is another line north of the Saskatchewan river, passing westerly south of Kindersley, between that and the south Saskatchewan river. This line stops east and about 20 or 25 miles south of Kindersley. Money has been borrowed on the bonds for the building of that road. I *cannot conceive that the money borrowed and lying in the bank is just enough to provide for construction exactly as far as the road happens to be built. That is

inconceivable, because they did not get the money mile by mile. I should like to know how far these two particular lines are covered by money that is earmarked for the completion of the line.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would involve an examination of the legislation authorizing the construction, and the trust deed under which the bonds were issued, whose proceeds my hon. friend has referred to. I have asked the Comptroller of Railways to obtain the information, and I suppose he will furnish it later.
If they have been able to arrive at a sum which would likely complete the road, surely they must know where the road will be when it is completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is quite possible the money they have in hand, representing the proceeds of the bonds, would not be sufficient to construct the railway which they had in contemplation when the project was entered upon, because of the increased cost of labour and material at the present time. I beg to move that the committee report progress.
Would the hon. minister adjourn the debate till Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have to obtain certain information, and we will proceed on Monday or Tuesday, when I hope we shall be able to make progress.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: With regard to the land damages in Montreal, arising out of the construction of the tunnel, has the Government any information as to the unsettled claims for damages? They amount to a very large sum, and I hope the Government will give us the information.

Much of the information asked for by the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is already contained in the Canadian Northern blue book. On page 10 of that book we have a list of the unguaranteed securities, as follows:
Mt. Royal T. & T., 5 per cent rent charge bonds, $9,191,366.72.
Those bonds are secured by mortgage on the rental, as I pointed out, equivalent to five per cent of that amount, and if my right hon. friend will turn to page 11 he will find that, in London, $790,000 of these bonds are hypothecated for loans there. There is none of them in Canada, but in New York, due on the 1st September this 
year, there is a loan of a million and three-quarters secured by the hypothecation of two and a half million of those securities, and that money is paying for these temporary structures.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Sir THOMAS WHITE moved the third reading of Bill No. 117, to authorize the levying of a war tax upon certain incomes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I hope the hon. minister will not take that up now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I understood it was agreeable to hon. gentlemen that we might proceed with the discussion of this Bill.

As I understand this matter, the hon. Minister of Finance has practically said that the income tax is being introduced in lieu of what is known as the
business profits war tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that is not correct.

As I understand the matter, the business wiar tax is to come to an end, and will not be continued after the end of the year.
.Sir THOMAS WHITE:	The business
profits war tax, by its terms, coimes to an end on December 31st of this year. When that measure was introduced, it was thought the war would be at an end by that time. I stated expressly the other day that we should tax abnormal business profits resulting from the war, and in the next Budget that I bring down we shall deal with that matter.
Can we take it in this way: that the present War Tax Profits Bill expires December 31, 1917?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By its terms.
Will there be a renewal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have stated that next year a taxation will be imposed on excess business profits. I stated also the other day that it might be necessary to make some allowance for necessary plant extensions, but I laid down the principle, as strongly as I could, that abnormal business profits due to the war must be abnormally taxed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I know that
Mr. Speaker, if he were here, would make .a ruling in respect to this motion. At eight o'clock, I assume that he will have something to say with regard to it. In the meantime, the discussion on the amendment may proceed.

I am aware, Sir, that the third reading of the Bill is not usually taken advantage of for an extended discussion, and in anything that I say to the House I shall keep that well in mind. I had not an opportunity of saying anything on the second reading of this Bill, and I should like to make one or two observations at this .stage.
A shrewd man said in his biography: " Nations seldom accept advice from individuals, however reasonable; they are taught less by theory than .by facts and events." If this House had been teachable by theory on a question of direct taxation, we should have had an income tax before

to-day, and I should have had some responsibility for its existence, because since I came to this House nine years ago I have taken frequent opportunities of pointing out the disadvantages of indirect taxation and the superiority of direct taxation. The war, however, has been a great fiscal .schoolmaster, as well as a great -schoolmaster along other lines, and personally, while I have something to say in the way of suggestion to the hon. minister, I -beg to offer him my hearty congratulations that-somewhat tardily, I am afraid^-he has learned from the course of the war the necessity of putting on some direct taxation.
I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) yesterday. He drew attention to one of the points of superiority of direct over indirect taxation when he very clearly said that direct taxation has a tendency to fall more upon the shoulders of the rich than upon the shoulders of the poor. In this w,ay it is diametrically opposed in its incidence to taxation of an indirect nature under a tariff, which, as a matter of fact, falls more upon the poor than upon the rich.
He might have gone on to point out another advantage of direct taxation, and a very great advantage in this regard. The minister has said that he anticipates that $20,000,000 will be raised under the Income Tax measure as he has introduced it in this House. If we were to raise that $20,000,000 *under a tariff, we should permit people within our own shores to take, for their own aggrandisement, two, three or perhaps four times that $20,000,000 out of the pockets of the taxpayers, at the same time that we got the paltry $20,000,000 for the *benefit of the State. That seems a very absurd way of raising the revenue of a country, and there is no controverting the fact that, when we take, let us say. $20,000,000 by duties on goods imported into the country, by raising the price of goods of a similar kind produced in the country, we at the same time transfer two or throe or four times that $20,000,000 from the Dockets of the consumers into the pockets of those incidentally protected by the customs tariff. That, with the advantage pointed out by my hon. friend from Kingston, would seem to me to be enough to convince any reasonable body of legislators that there are very great advantages in direct taxation over those possessed by indirect taxation.
fMr. M. CIarlc.1
I want, however, to do the Minister of Finance the obvious credit of saying that I think, so far as my knowledge of the history of Canada goes, he is the first Minister of Finance who has raised any direct taxation in the Federal Parliament, and, .after all, it is but bare justice to do him that credit. He deserves credit to that extent, and he has earned that credit, not always with the encouragement which he has a right to expect from every one in war time. When the minister introduced his excess profits taxation, I remember the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), night after night, castigating my hon. friend for introducing the tax. I am sure the minister remembers that also.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He does.

That does not represent the full measure of the hardness of the minister's case, because when he proceeded to carry out his previous promise by which he was bound to let the tax lapse at a certain period, just as my hon. friend from Pictou had pursued him with horse, foot and artillery, for putting the tax on, so my hon. friend from North . Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) pursued him with horsd, foot and artillery for taking the tax off. I do not think it is possible to conceive of any Minister of Finance, unless he had gifts superior to those of human beings, pleasing two critics holding such diametrically opposite views. The surpassing ability of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as a leader is shown by the fact that he gathers both those followers holding diametrically opposite views under the capacious shadow of his own garment. I hope this will not be taken in bad part, because I do not mean it so.
For of such is the Kingdom of Heaven. His followers come from the East and from the West.

The House is
shortly to be called upon to consider an amendment which proposes to increase the ' amount of tax that shall be levied under this Income Tax Bill on those of larger incomes. I want to put in a plea for that organization with which I have been connected for the last three years. I would ask the members of the House Seriously to consider how an increase in the tax upon higher incomes will affect those who have entered upon serious obligations of their own accord. If it were proposed that the income tax rate on higher incomes should be made greater to cover the year 1918, I would raise no objection. I quite concur in what has been said, that those who have the money during these times should be the ones to contribute as much as they possibly can. But I would call the attention of the

House to this. The income tax which will be payable, on lelt June next will be based on a statement filed on 28th February, 1918, covering the income of the year 1917. Now, during the year 1917, the people of Canada have taken upon themselves (voluntarily very large obligations. Never in the history of the war has there been a year in which the -siibscripltions to various war charities have been so generous and so universal as in the year 1917. During the year many and many a man has asked himself the question, "How much can I possibly do without in order that I may put my name down for the largest possible amount for one of the war funds?" Many of these men have voluntarily reduced to a very considerable extent that portion of their income which they are free to spend upon themselves, not in any wiay anticipating that an income tax would 'be brought in by Parliament this year. Now, I contend that you are going to place upon these men a double burden. They have already of their own accord assumed a heavy load, and you are going to lay upon them a still greater burden.
There are a few people in this country-very few, I am glad to say-who have not given of their means to the Patriotic Fund and other war charities, but have hoarded *and held all they had 'and all they could make. These men are held up again and again to the contempt and scorn of their fellow-citizens, and are receiving only-what they deserve in the way of contumely. I do not care how heavily they may be taxed! but I want to testify on behalf of the Canadian people that for one man of that kind, there are twenty who are contributing generously and have been doing so since the war began. In every community wheTe a campaign has been conducted our attention has been drawn to one or two men who will give nothing, but you can at the same time secure a list, if you care to, of a score of men who are denying themselves daily in order that they may give. When the history of this war comes to be written there will be no brighter page in the whole record than that which records the efforts to do something that have been made by those who, for various reasons, could not go. to the front, but who endeavoured in their turn to do all they could to back up the men on the firing line. That spirit has been practically universal from one end of the Dominion to the other, not a single province excepted.
It has been my duty since the war began to act as a sort of apostle to the stay-11 Sir Herbert Ames.]
at-homes. I was six years beyond the military age, and physically unfit to enlist, and as I could not go to the front I gave my whole time to another work which was the best I could get under the circumstances. During the past three years I .have travelled up .and down this country again and again from Halifax to Vancouver, and have spoken in every city and town of considerable size in the whole Dominion, and 1 want to say that universally the people of Canada have been ready -and willing to make sacrifices. Again and again we have asked communities to give us not only all they needed for themselves, but something over which might be spent in more hard-pressed districts, and with the exception of five towns in Ontario-Sarnia, Preston, Orillia, Fort WTilliam and Kenora- every area that I know of in the province of Ontario has given not only what it needed for itself, but an additional sum to be spent out in Alberta and Saskatchewan, in the far West and along the Pacific coast. If any one had told me at the beginning of the war that the Patriotic Fund would be able to raise between $5,000,000 and $6,000,000, I would have confessed that I did not believe a larger sum was possible, yet a fair computation to-day will show that there has been raised for the various war charities in Canada since the war began between $50,000,000 and $60,000,000 in money and food supplies, not one dollar of which would have been raised had not the hearts of our people been right. Our generosity has been an astonishment to ourselves; it has been a stimulus to our neighbours to the south of us, and has been the subject of congratulation from other parts of the Empire. I think that this year alone no less a sum than $20,000,000 has been pledged and will be paid by the people of Canada out of their revenues to the various war funds which are well known to us all.
Last fall we reached the apex of our demands. The Manitoba Patriotic Fund, although independent of ours, works on exactly the same lines and is in constant touch with us, so that when I give figures regarding the Patriotic Fund I give figures for Manitoba also. Last fall we realized that we had about 65,000 families to look after, scattered throughout the Dominion. The fundamental principle of the Patriotic Fund has always been that every community should raise what it could, and put that sum into a common purse, to be dispensed in each district according to need.

Some 01 me wealthy districts of the East that sent comparatively few men were able to send a considerable surplus of money to districts in the West that had sent nearly every available man of military age, and in that way the burden has been distributed. We realized, however, that we should have to meet during the year 1917 a monthly expenditure of approximately $1,000,000. We could not Think for a moment of allowing our soldiers' dependents to be in need this year, and so we carefully prepared our campaign. We alloted to each province, and to every part of each province, what we considered to be its fair share, and there is not a province in the whole Dominion but has given the full amount asked for. The result has been that we have already received in cash $8,500,000 in the first six months of this year.
We have another eight and a half million dollars due and payable during the remainder of this year, and considerable sums payable in January and February.
My contention is that people having voluntarily assumed large burdens for the year 1917, called upon as they will be to pay this income tax in addition at the rates already specified, they should not, at least in the first instance, be overburdened with an excessive amount. It is not fair to imagine that a man's whole income for 1917 remains with him, apart from the amount which may be taken out of him by this income tax. The first year of the war, 1915, we took in about $6,000,000, 85 per cent of which came from voluntary subscriptions. On analyzing it we found that the rural districts were not giving as freely as the cities. We found the reason to be that it was very much more difficult to organize campaigns in the rural sections than in the cities, not that there was any less willingness to give in the rural communities. We had recourse to the county councils, and wherever a county council was willing to make a unanimous appropriation and levy its contribution as a tax, we regarded it as a voluntary gift. We received a large amount in this way. Of the $15,000,000 or $16,000,000 we expect to receive during the present year, 63 per cent is voluntary, 16 per cent comes from provincial grants, 15 per cent from county council grants, rand 6 per cent from various municipalities, that is, the grants of city councils and so on Last winter, when we made these campaigns, we told all those who subscribed that we wanted them to pay upon a monthly basis.
We told them if peace was declared they would not have to pay any further subscriptions after the date of peace negotiations, for it was our endeavour to keep on hand a sufficient surplus to take care of the returned men for a time after peace was actually declared. So, we have a large number of these continuing subscriptions coming in to us in very considerable amounts from month to month. Our revenue is almost uniform. Every month is practically the same as the preceding month.
