It is very popular, indeed, to talk about the sacrifices of the poor man, and let me pay a tribute to the working people of the Dominion of Canada, who, from one end of the country to the other, are giving us their day's pay, sometimes a day's pay a year, sometimes a day's pay each quarter, and somfr times a day every month. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been paid in to us, taken each month out of the pay envelopes of the working men of Canada. The working men of Canada, however, are not the only ones who are making sacrifices. The rich men of the country are also making sacrifices. More than once I have heard men say " I do not want to have one dollar more when this war is over than I had when it began, and every dollar I have in the way of surplus, I give it to some patriotic fund." I know of other men who have cut down their living to as economical a basis as they can, in order that they may give large subscriptions, and any campaign committee in any city will tell you they are absolutely surprised at the sums men supposed to have only normal incomes are willing to deprive themselves of in order to give to those funds. Many men are giving a very large percentage of their incomes at the present time, in the full expectation that that would constitute their main war contribution for 1917. When you say that a man with an income of $10,000, for instance, has practically all of his income left, do not forget that he may have already promised to give out of that income for patriotic purposes a very much larger sum than the tax gatherer proposes to collect from him. Not everybody in Canada is a profiteer. Not every wealthy man is rolling in wealth because of this war. There are a great many industries in this 'Country that are not making money and there are a great many men reputed as wealthy who were never so poor in their lives as during this war, yet these men are giving generously and saying nothing about it. The percent-



age of those who make extreme profits is small, taking Canada as a whole. I would be the last to defend these people in the smallest degree. Where abnormal profits are being made from munitions, or from any other source, I would vote to take a very large share of those profits. At the same time, we should not consider that every man reputed to be fairly comfortably off has become a millionaire from day to day during this war.
This income tax is new. It is more or less experimental. It seems to me, in view of the fact that it was unexpected, it should not be made excessive. We should consider the obligations people have already voluntarily assumed for 1917. In all probability, it will be necessary to re-impose this tax, because the war will not end in a few months. Either the present Finance Minister, or some other Finance Minister, will within twelve months have to deal with the tax again, and probably will increase the rate on . the higher incomes. People will not complain if that be done for the year 1918, because they see it coming, and can make their arrangements accordingly. If I am fortunate enough to be here in 1918, and it is then proposed to place a larger tax on the higher incomes, I, for one, shall raise no objection. I wish, however, to say to the Finance Minister that if the tax is increased he must expect that the Patriotic Fund will not receive as much as it has received up to the present, and it may be necessary for him to add $10,000,000 to his income tax in order that that sum may be given to the Patriotic Fund. I do not believe that after a heavy income tax is introduced, we shall be able to get from voluntary giving anything like the sums we are to-day receiving. We shall probably continue the organization, and we shall probably endeavour to utilize those sources of revenue which the income tax will not affect, but since our revenues come largely from givers in the cities, I do not think those other sources will be sufficient for our needs. We had voluntary campaigns not long ago in connection for the needs of the current year. Montreal gave us $3,000,000; Toronto, outside of York county, gave us $2,500,000; Hamilton, $650,000; Ottawa, $400,000; London, $300,000; Brockville, $150,000; St. Catharines, $100,000; Halifax, $200,000; Vancouver, $400,000; Victoria, $200,000; Edmonton, $150,000; Calgary, $175,000; Quebec, $250,000. The greater part of this money is voluntarily subscribed and is being paid monthly, and will not all be paid up for another eight or nine months.

Speaking again of the men of wealth, I feel we should put on record some of the noble gifts they have made since the war began . We well remember the gift of $500,000 made by Mr. J. K. L. *Ross. I heard indirectly that Mr. I rules Carruthere, of Montreal, had given to various war funds about $200,000 since the outbreak of hostilities. Mr. A. Hamilton Gault gave $100,000 for the P.P.C.L.I. Here are several men whose gifts, I know have gone into six figures since the war began: Sir Edmund Osier, Sir Edward Kemp, Sir Herbert Holt, Mr. Huntley Drummond, the Bilks' of Montreal and the Ross', of Quebec. These men men have all given in the most generous possible manner. I have a list here of our subscribers in Montreal and I see that 240 men have given $508,000. I could put the names on Hansard if it was desired but I see that it is just six o'clock. I have a list here of .thirty-one men in Toronto who gave $143,500. In London thirty-three men gave $135,000. Hamilton also has been very generous. I trust that, whatever the future may bring for the patriotic fund, the present relief organization may be continued. We are administering a million dollars a month at no cost whatever to the subscribers inasmuch as the interest on our bank balance pays all the cost of administration from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We have been able to isecure this year $15,000,000 at a cost of less than one-third of bne per cent for the raising of it. We have a voluntary staff in every part of Canada, composed of people who are taking up this work for the love of the cause and who are endeavouring in that way to do their bit. I trust that whatever this or .any government may do it will not break up the existing relief machinery which is running so smoothly. My plea to this House in connection with the income tax is that it should remember the voluntary obligations which have been assumed by the people of Canada for the year 1917 and that, if it is planning to make the tax fall more heavily upon the larger givers, this may be postponed for another year.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

I
wish to make a few remarks, and as the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross), who had the floor at six o'clock is not present, I may as well proceed.

I agree with a great deal of what has been said commending the action, of the hon. Minister of Finance in bringing down a measure providing for an income tax. I think the principle of the measure is desirable from many points of view. It is direct taxation, and, therefore, it is definite. Those who pay know how much they are paying, and the money is paid into the treasury. It is not the same as a tariff imposition, under which for every dollar paid into the treasury two or more dollars are paid into the pockets of those who have the 'benefits of the tariff provision. To that extent I desire, therefore, to add my support, to that which the Finance Minister has already received. . But, when I agree with the principle and the desirability of establishing a principle, I am also compelled to follow the criticism that has been made by other members on this side, in recognizing that the upward graduation of the tax as the hon. minister proposes it does not appear to me to be adequate, considering the circumstances in which we are placed to-day. In these special circumstances, when extraordinary expenditures are being made, when debt is being piled up as it is to-day, it appears to me that there should be a heavier levy on the larger incomes than is imposed by the measure now before the House. To that extent I would agree with those who have taken exception to the measure. I am also compelled to agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), that it is unfortunate and undesirable that it should be held out to the country that in consideration of the imposition of the income tax, there is contemplated, or may be contemplated a remission of the excess profits tax. It is true the excess profits tax has been criticised from varying points of view, It has been said, of course, that no taxation is pleasing, and that it is an easy matter to find fault -with any form of taxation, and no doubt the excess profits tax imposed by the Minister of Finance a couple of years ago has points and features that press unequally or unfairly, and is capable of great improvement. At the same time, I am sure the Finance Minister must recognize that, from this side, speaking generally, he received support for the principle of the excess profits tax. There was disagreement as to details, but I do not think there was any disagreement as to the principle that there should be such a tax. Some people objected that it was excessive, but I 294}
am compelled to take the view that it was below the mark rather than in excess, considering the circumstances in which we are placed. It was imposed especially as a war measure, as I understood the matter. It proposed to deal with a condition which existed, in which excessive profits were reaped because of the existence of war. It is only natural, right and proper, that when such excessive profits are being reaped by reason of the existence of war, and when it is obvious that these excessive profits must cease when the war ceases, there should be excessive or extreme taxation upon these profits in order to balance the situation; that is to say, a heavy tax on excess profits, and especially on war profits* is a proper measure of taxation at this time. And if it is contemplated, as it *appears to be, that the excess profits tax shall cease, to be replaced by the present, income tax, I consider that to be exceedingly objectionable legislation. I consider that the principle involved in the remission of the excess profits tax is a bad principle, and that that remission is not balanced by the imposition of the income tax. It has been said here to-day that the advantage of the income tax, or of any direct tax, is that it can be made to bear more heavily upon the wealthy than upon the people of ordinary means, whereas a tariff tax must bear more heavily upon the man of lesser than upon the man of greater means. For that reason, looked at from a proper economic standpoint, the income tax is essentially a desirable form of taxation. But when we find that the special taxation taken from war profits and levied because of war conditions is to be abrogated, and in the place of that is established an income tax, which, being lightly graduated upward, rests more heavily, in proportion, upon the men of lesser income than upon the men of greater income, I can only take the view that the minister, while adopting a sound principle, has not given that principle the effect that should be given to it.
We must have money to carry on the business of the country. If that money does not come from one source, it must come from another. If it does not come from the excess profits of those who are fortunate under war conditions, if it does not come from the man with large income* then it must come from the man with a small income, either through the income tax or through the exactions of the tariff. This is a tim-e and an occasion in the history of this country during which, while-there has been a vast outpouring of money

into the lap of Canada, those who are dependent upon their labour, whether of hand or of brain-that is to say, whether the artisan who works for wages or the office man who works for what he is pleased to call salary-are, by the cost of living, subjected to a heavier burden than they have ever before been called upon to bear. That is to say, owing to the advance in the cost of the necessaries of life the man who receives a fixed salary or a fixed wage is closer up to the limit than he e%rer was before. That being the case, this is not the time to increase either directly or indirectly the burdens upon that section of the community. Whatever increased burden of taxation is imposed should be levied upon those who are able to bear it; upon the man who is reaping excessive profits out of war conditions or the man who by reason of good fortune is in the enjoyment of the larger income and therefore can spare a greater proportion of that income to assist in the upkeep of the country during these strenuous times. The man of smaller salary necessarily has to spend that salary in order to live; the burden of taxation upon that man is greater in proportion, although much less in amount, than that whibh rests upon the man of the larger salary. A single man in receipt of say $1,500 or $2,000 or a man with family in receipt of $3,000 a year has but a small margin, between the cost of living and the amount of his salary; that is, according to the ordinary standard of living. I do not wish to be understood as saying that the single man receiving $1,500 or married m.an receiving $3,000 a year should not pay income tax; I quite agree that he should pay income tax; but, as compared with - the amount paid by the man who has an income of say $10,000, the amount of the tax imposed upon him is necessarily out of proportion to the difference between his salary and his experises. The man with the $10,000 income can cut down his expenses without unreasonably reducing his standard of living, but the man with the $2,000 salary cannot cut down his living expenses without seriously affecting his standard of living. There is room for the talcing of the larger proportion from those whose incomes are greatest.
In following out the schedule submitted by the Finance Minister it cannot be argued that the proportion taken from a man of large means bears the same relation to the difference between his cost of living and his revenue as in the case of the man with the smaller income. That, I think, should be remedied; it is a condition that mili-

tates seriously against the merit of the proposals of the Finance Minister. I want to make this suggestion. It is borne in upon the people that the cost of living has tremendously increased in recent years. It has increased by one-half in four years, while salaries and wages have not increased in anything like that proportion. While I make the plea that the heavier burden be laid upon the man of larger means, I also make the plea that the tariff should be reduced so that the burden would be* lightened upon the man of lesser means. The man almost the whole of whose ifacome must be spent in maintaining himself and his family should have some measure of relief by a decrease in the customs tariff on the necessaries of life. An increase of revenue should be taken from those who can afford to pay it and the burden of the high cost of living should be lifted in some measure from those who are . less able to pay. This country is going up against the wall, so to speak. The cost of living is increasing. Taxation is necessarily increasing, and the means of meeting that high cost of living and that increase of taxation are not being provided, notwithstanding the enormous outpouring of wealth into the lap of Canada as a result of the war. I would urge, therefore, that the income tax measure should- not displace the war profits tax; that the war profits tax should be increased; that the income tax should be graduated more steeply in its higher figures, and that the tariff should be reduced with a view to reducing the cost of living to those whose outlay is necessarily within such a close margin of their income.
I was attracted by the plea made by the member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) for consideration, in the imposition of the income tax, of those men of wealth who have contributed liberally to the Patriotic Fund. There is, I think, some merit in"lhe hon. member's contention. The purpose of the Patriotic Fund is essentially a national purpose. It makes provision that is an absolute necessity to the credit of the country and to the maintenance of -Canada's position in regard to the war. I have never looked upon the Canadian Patriotic Fund as -something that should be a matter of private enterprise. I have -always looked upon it as something that should be borne by the nation and that -should be dealt with by the nation. I was never able to understand why there should be paid out of the Dominion treasury to the dependents of the

soldier overseas a separation allowance that is admittedly less than is requisite to provide those dependents with a decent livelihood. Whatever amount is reasonably necessary to maintain the dependents of the soldier overseas should be provided out of the Dominion treasury, and anything less than that is not doing justice to the soldier and is not creditable to the country. There is plenty of work for an organization such as the Canadian Patriotic Fund in taking care of special instances of difficulty or hardship that necessarily result because of men leaving their families and going to serve their country. I have heard the hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) argue that it is not possible for a Government to take care of the many exceptional cases that must necessarily arise, and that, therefore, there is a reason for the existence and administration of the Canadian Patriotic Fund. I quite agree with 'that. That, however, is not the point. The point is that the Canadian Patriotic Fund, under certain circumstances, pays to the dependents of the soldier a fixed amount, and my contention is that that fixed amount should be paid out of the Dominion treasury.

It is not a fixed amount; it is a variable amount, and that is the crux of the whole situation. The Government cannot discriminate, but the Canadian Patriotic Fund can. The Government can consider the dependents only as appanages of the men and the Government has to give the families through the men the same sum, whether they need it or not, no matter what the cost of living or the size of the family may be. The Canadian Patriotic Fund approaches the matter from an entirely different angle. It looks into the case of each family separately. It does not take the soldier into consideration at all. It simply says: How much is needed, in addition to the existing income of the family to bring that income up to the scale of decent subsistence for that family, and the sum differs in every province. I would be glad to-night, or .at any other time, to hand to the hon. member the monthly statements for April, May and June, and he will see from them that, in no two places in the Dominion of Canada, is exactly the same amount given to families differently circumstanced. There are no two places in Canada where there are identical conditions. In Prince Edward Island we give to the average family $10.24 per month; in Nova Scotia,
$11.83; in New Brunswick, $13.87; in Newfoundland, $13.14; in Ontario, $15.03; in Quebec, $16.17; in Saskatchewan, $22.58. We give twice as much in Saskatchewan as we do in Prince Edward Island because the cost of living in Saskatchewan is considerably higher than it is in Prince Edward Island. We give to the average family in Southern Alberta $19.10 per month, and in Northern Alberta, $19.58; in greater Vancouver, $20.25; in Victoria city, $21.54; and in British Columbia generally, $20.79 per month.
The point I am taking is this, that the Government cannot discriminate-if the Speaker will allow me to finish this matter with the hon. member for Edmonton-between families. It will have to give the soldiers' family in Prince Edward Island the same amount that it gives the soldier's family in Alberta, and if it were to do that, it would be giving to families - in Prince Edward Island a great deal more than they required. The only way in which the Government could satisfy every one by an indiscriminate method would be to give the maximum rate throughout Canada, and in that case it would be giving a great deal more than would be needed by the families in some of the provinces. We have estimated that we do for about $12,000,000 what the Government could not do for less than $20,000,000, because in each case we discriminate according to locality and according to the needs of each individual family; and if, in doing that, we can save $8,000,000 a year, and, at the same time, bring the families up to a decent state of subsistence, it is surely better that we should do that work than that the Government should do it.

I cannot altogether agree with the position taken by my hon. friend. My point is that if it takes $30 a month to provide decent subsistence for the dependents of a soldier in Prince Edward Island, the Government should pay that $30, and if it takes $40 to provide decent subsistence for the dependents of a soldier in Alberta, the Government should pay that $40. There is no reason why the Government should not discriminate between province and province in the payment of separation allowances for soldiers, any more than there is reason why it should not discriminate in the payment of salaries of its officials; and, as a matter of fact, it does discriminate in regard to the salaries of its officials. There are certain allowances paid in western Canada that are not paid in eastern Canada in the public service of the conn-

try, and there is no reason why there should not be a similar discrimination between province and province in the payment of separation allowances. As to discrimination between families, once you bring the payment from the public treasury up to what is admittedly required for the decent subsistence of the family, then the work of the Piatriotic Fund comes in, and if there are special cases, then there is room and opportunity for those people who are desirous of showing their benevolence and who take an interest in the welfare of our soldiers and their dependents to exercise that benevolence, care and supervision about which my hon. friend speaks, and which I do not 'wish for one moment to belittle in any way. When it is recognized that a certain fixed amount is necessary as reasonable subsistence to the dependents of the soldier, that sum should be paid out of the Dominion treasury. It is the country that the 'soldier is serving, not his neighbours particularly, nor those who are of patriotic o>r benevolent mind, and the country should pay whatever is right and proper for the maintenance of his dependents. If the present rate of taxation is not sufficient for that purpose, then the rate of taxation should be increased until it is sufficient. Perhaps this is not an appropriate time to discuss the merits of the Patriotic Fund, 'but my hon. friend (Sir Herbert Ames) favoured the House with his views in regard to the matter, and I have taken the liberty of following him to this extent.
I said, in the beginning of my remarks, that I was quite willing to agree that those men of wealth, who had contributed liberally and who were still contributing liberally to the Patriotic Fund, should have their contributions recognized as part of their income tax-bufr only if the whole of the money required for the maintenance of the dependents of the soldiers is taken from the Dominion treasury, as, in my judgment, it should be taken.
I do not desire to withhold in any way the credit that is due to the men of wealth who have contributed of their means to the maintenance of the dependents of soldiers, and I certainly would not wish to see them taxed double, but I would like to see those men of wealth who have not contributed as they should have done made to contribute either through a war profits tax or an income tax or in some other way, so that they may pay their share of the obligation that rests upon them as citizens. I do not,want to detract in any way from- the work my 
hon. friend has done or from the good-will of those who have made the contributions, but I say ithat the system of making the dependents of our soldiers subject to the control and direction and at the mercy of an organization that stands where the country should stand, tends (to lower the standing of our soldiers and their dependents, tends to depress the patriotic enthusiasm that caused those men to volunteer and, in its moral effect, is an injury, and I am compelled to say an injustice to the men and their dependents. I hope that what I am saying will not be considered as any reflection upon the good intent of everybody concerned, but I say that you cannot make men and women and children subject to that which of necessity has the appearance of charity, without lessening their self-respect, and when you do that you take away what is best in them and do them irreparable harm when you are really trying to do them good.
My suggestion is that the contributions of the rich to the Patriotic Fund should be recognized in the income tax, but that the burden now carried by the Patriotic Fund should be carried direct by the Dominion treasury, and if it is necessary the income tax and the war profits tax should be increased in order that that money may be paid ouit of the treasury.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With respect to the
amendment moved this afternoon by the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), section 54 of the British North America Act, the rules, and the invariable practice of this House, prescribe that any motion which is designed to levy a tax can only be introduced by a minister on the previous recommendation of the Crown. The amendment of the hon. member for West Lambton, if it has any object at all, is designed to levy an increased charge upon the people, and is 'therefore, for the reasons I have indicated, clearly out of order.

I just wish to refer you, Sir, to page 431 of Bourinot which says:
All the authorities go to show that, when the Government have formally submitted to the House the question for the revision of customs and' excise duties, it is competent for a member "to propose in committee to substitute another tax of equivalent amount for that proposed by ministers, the necessity of new taxation to a given extent being declared on behalf of the Crown.''
It is also competent for any member to propose another scheme of taxation for the same purpose, as a substitute for the Government plan.
Read the next sentence.

But it is not regular to propose a new and distinct tax, which is not a mere increase or diminution of' a duty upon an article already recommended by Government for taxation, though it is the function of this committee to impose rather than to repeal taxes.
I submit that my amendment proposes to the Government the same scheme of taxation they have" themselves proposed, but in a larger form. I would also point out that the amendment simply asks that this scheme of taxation be submitted with the Government's approval. It asks nothing further than that. I .submit that I am doing exactly what Bourinot says it is competent for any member to do, namely, " to propose another scheme of taxation for the same purpose, as a substitute for the Government plan." Bourinot gives his authorities in a foot note on the same page. I am simply proposing the same scheme of taxation in a larger form, and I am asking that it be done with the consent of the Government, and that the Bill be referred back to the committee. With all deference to you, Sir, I therefore submit that the amendment is in order, because Bourinot expressly states that while it is not regular for a member to propose an entirely different scheme of taxation, it is competent for him' to propose another scheme of taxation for the same purpose, although it is in a larger measure.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext: May I ask you, Sir, to rule upon the point that I am asking the Bill to be referred back with the approval of the Government?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may say to the hon. member that after consulting the authorities I have not been able to ascertain that in any instance the consent of the Government has been given to a motion of this character being made by a private member, and except it should be so it would not be in order.

I must, of course, bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. At the same time I believe that the clause within the resolution which only refers it to the House, or to the committee, with the approval of the Government-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Government would first have to obtain the approval of the Crown.

The hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), in discussing the measure before the House, pointed out what he apprehended as a menace to the future success of the Patriotic Fund, which has been under his charge since its inception, and which he has undoubtedly administered to the general satisfaction of the Canadian public. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has dealt with the observations of the member for St. Antoine, and has taken the position that the benevolence administered through the medium of the Patriotic Fund is an obligation which the Government should assume and administer. With that view I concur. I also desire to point out to the House that a couple of years ago, when speaking in the debate upon the Address, I took the position that all these funds should be in the charge of the Government, that all moneys to be paid out on account of the war should be

raised and distributed by the Government, and that no part of the work should be left to private initiative, private benevolence or private administration. My hon. friend from St. Antoine has supported his view of the matter-a view to which his experience, I admit, gives great weight-by stating that if the fund were administered by the Government instead of as it is now administered, there would be an increased burden of $8,000,000 upon the country.

We have uncollected balances, arising from pledges which have been made, which we expect will yield us from $8,500,000 to $10,000,000 in the course of the next nine months. Until those pledges are paid, it seems to me it would be double taxation to assess unduly the persons who are paying those large sums of money.

That is not exactly the point to which I allude. I understood if the work were taken over by the Government, it would cost the country many millions more than it is now costing-some $8,000,000 I think my hon. friend said.

Yes, in this way. In the first place this fund is administered without any expanse whatever, inasmuch as the interest pays the administration expenses; in the second place, by being able to discriminate between families, and only give a family the supplementary assistance necessary to bring it up to the scale of decent subsistence in the particular locality, we are able to vary the sums we give to families in different provinces, whereas my contention is the Government would have to treat every family from one end of Canada to the other in exactly the same way, just as a soldier's pay has to be the same whether he comes from Prince Edward Island or from the Yukon. If the Government took it over, the supplementary grant would have to be sufficient to meet the highest requirements of the most expensive province, and if that were done we estimate it would cost the Government about $21,000,000 to do what we are doing for about $12,000,000.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I hope the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) will not enlarge upon the discussion on the Patriotic Fund.
It had a bearing, inasmuch as the hon. member for St. Antoine referred to it as one of the reasons why the amendment of the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) should not be adopted on the ground that it would take a larger share 
from the larger incomes. It has not the same bearing upon the discussion of the third reading of the Bill. While I do not wish to restrict the hon. member unduly, I hope he will make his remarks upon the Patriotic Fund as brief as possible.

I promise I will not infringe upon the time of the House at any length with reference to this matter. I may, however, be permitted to conclude my observations on the point by saying that I do not admit the last position taken by my hon. friend (Sir Herbert Ames), and it is rather surprising to me that he should offer such a candid criticism of the administration of affairs by the Government. I would commend the methods of my hon. friend to the Government, particularly the one _ by which he says the cost of administration is defrayed by the interest he is able to secure upon the principal fund collected.
Now, just a word or two with reference to this Bill. I do not question your ruling, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the amendment offered by the member for West Lambton. I regre't it was not within the rules of the House, and that the object sought by my hon. friend could not have been attained in that way, but still the same end may be attained if the Minister of Finance will forget his difficulties with the Canadan Northern Railway Bill and be receptive to the advice which has been tendered him in connection with this measure. He can surely do this of his own motion. The amendment of my hon. friend from West Lambton merely asked the committee to apply in practical operation two principles-first, that taxes should be levied upon those best able to pay them; and, second, that in the case of this particular Bill, a greater burden should be laid upon those in receipt of large incomes. Leaving aside my hon. friend's amendment, I may point out that the Bill itself brings up the whole question of the taxation methods adopted by the Government, and the result to be obtained therefrom, and necessarily causes us to take public opinion into consideration with regard to the Government's methods of taxation and with respect to the results which have accrued from the application of those methods. I desire to place before the House two views upon this aspect of the matter. One of these views I wish to present from a Canadian standpoint, and the other from the standpoint of a recognized authority in the United States. If the Minister of Finance

will not hearken to the advice that is tendered to him in all friendliness from this side of the House, it occurred to me that possibly he might give ear to the advice that rpay be obtained for him from the pages of a Government publication. I hold in my hand a small pamphlet on the title page of which I read:
For Free Distribution.
National Organization for War. by Stephen Leacock. Reprinted for the National Service Board' of Canada.
On the back of the cover there are various mottoes encouraging national thrift, national saving, and national investment. I might explain that this pamphlet contains an article written by Mr. Stephen Leacock. The National Service Board of Canada, a creation of the present Government, and presided over by my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. R. B. Bennett), thought so much of the advice given in this article of Mr. Leacock's that they had it reprinted and distributed as a government pamphlet. That being so, and in case my hon. friend the Minister of Finance may not be familiar with the contents of this pamphlet, I desire to quote from it briefly so that he may know what practically another branch of the Government, of which he is a member, thinks of the method and the measure of his taxation. After an introduction dealing with the war and the position of affairs in this country under war, this pamphlet says-page 3:
To and fro we go about our business. We pay our easy taxes, and subscribe to our so-called patriotic loan, so issued that the hungriest money-lender in New York is glad to clamor for a share of it.
Then this National Service Board pamphlet lays down a certain principle in regard to the war tax, and in the course of what it has to say on this point, I find the following dictum:
The so-called' War Tax is but a small part of a man's earnings.
After discussing that principle at some length, the pamphlet proceeds:
War brings with it the peculiar phenomenon of war prosperity.
Then the author, who is so highly thought of by the National Service Board as to have his pamphlet officially adopted for circulation in Canada, applies this dictum to the Dominion of Canada, and having made the application, he proceeds thus:
In and through it all moves smug hpyocrisy, suggesting the little words and phrases that are to salve the soul; teaching the manufacturer to call himself a patriot as he pockets his private gains, and to shout for trade, more trade, that he may cram his pockets the fuller; teaching the farmer that his own fat, easy industry is war itself, and that he may count his fatted cattle in the light of his stable lantern and go to bed a patriot; teaching all the drones and parasites, the lawyers, the professors, the chefs and the piano-players, the actors and the buffoons that in going on with their business they are aiding in the conduct of the war.
1 think, Mr. Speaker, you will admit that that is a very candid criticism of one branch of the government of the day by another branch. If I were to adopt it as expressing my own views, I would say that it leaves nothing for me to add to the criticism on that point. It follows that criticism by presenting, through the National Service Board, to the Government, what should he the real war policy. It goes on to say:
Every cent of the money that can he gathered up by national thrift should be absorbed by .national taxes and national loans. Our present taxes are, for war time, ridiculously low, as far as all people of comfortable, or even of decent, means are concerned. And they are made with one eye on the supposed benefit to industry.
The author of this pamphlet goes further and suggests a policy in regard to loans:
Over above the taxes we need a succession of Government patriotic loans, not money-lenders' loans at market and' supermarket rates, but patriotic loans in the real sense, at a low rate of interest, let us say four per cent, and issued in bonds of twenty-five dollars, with a dollar a year as interest.
But, in addition to this advice which is tendered by one branch of the Government to the other, the author further enjoins the absolute necessity of practising economy, and that is done in this way:
But first let the Government-of the dominions, the provinces, the cities and the towns-itself begin the campaign of thrift. At present vast sums of money are being wasted in so-called public works, railways in the wilderness, cement sidewalks in the streets, post offices in the towns-millions and millions that drain away our economic strength. In times of peace these are excellent. For war, unless they have a war purpose, the things are worse than useless. The work of the men who labour at them is of no value, and the food and clothes that they consume must he made by other men.
I do not think, if I took up the time of the House for the rest of this sitting, I could add anything to the excellent advice given to th? Government, and particularly to the Minister of Finance, by the National Service Board of 'Canada through this pamphlet circulated by the National Service Board, of which my hon. friend from Cal-

gary (Mr. E. B. Bennett) is the distinguished 'chairman. That is a home view, a view at close hand, of the method and measure of the taxation for which the Minister of Finance has stood sponsor.
It may be of interest to the House, and will I am sure (be of interest to the Minister of Finance, to hear very briefly the view which is entertained in the -adjoining republic of his taxation measures, and particularly of the one which is now before this House. In the Montreal Gazette of Monday -last I noticed an article dealing with a pamphlet which has been issued by Mr. Otto H. Kahn of Kahn, Loeb and'Com-pany on the subject of the war tax. In the course of that pamphlet the' writer lays down this principle:
The cost of the war must be laid according to the capacity to bear it.
Mr. Kahn goes1 on to discuss the measure which is now before this -House, and in the course of his analysis of it, he has this to say:
Within -the last few days it has been announced that the Canadian Government has introduced a Bill for the imposition of an income tax. The rates proposed are moderate for a war tax, the highest percentage of taxation being considerably less than one-half the rates fixed by our House of Representatives.
Moreover, the Act as introduced by the Government provides that income -taxation will be remitted to individuals up to the amount which they are now paying directly or as members of a co-partnership or as shareholders in corporations, for excess war profits, taxes and other special war taxes' under the existing law.
In fact, if the newspaper reports are correct, it is the announced intention of the Canadian Government with addition of the income tax, to reduce or abolish the excess profits tax at the end of the present year. Accordingly, while America, under the Bill pending in Congress, would provide an unprecedently high income tax, and excess profits tax, Canada would have hut a moderate income tax, and that tax apparently would not be in addition to, but largely or entirely in place of the excess profits tax.
The enrichment of corporations or persons out of profits resulting from a war in which this country is engaged is rightly abhorrent to the public conscience.
I commend that criticism from a recognized financial authority to the consideration of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. I do so for the reason that there seems to be an impression that the taxation in this country is as high as that in the United States. According to the statement of Mr. Kahn, it only approximates about one-half of the rates provided in the measure now before Congress.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Our business
profits taxation is very much heavier.
Mr. MUEPHY The hon. gentleman says it is very much heavier, but he himself is authority for the statement that tha-t tax is to be discontinued.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I stated two or three times that the profits tax is to be continued, and that it will be dealt with in the next Budget.
After this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After this year. This tax, by its terms, comes to an end December 31, and I stated this afternoon, as I have stated on several occasions recently, that when this tax was proposed it was thought the war would be -at an end by next December.
The hon. minister says this tax will be continued, and will be dealt with in the next Budget?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is there to be another Budget this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, next year.
How can the hon. minister give a guarantee as to next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know who can give a better guarantee.
My hon. friend expects to be here next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

All I can say is that my hon. friend is very much alone in that view. However, we have more serious business to transact at the present time. I commend the criticisms that I have submitted to my hon. friend's very careful consideration, and I hope that even before his next Budget to which he alludes he will provide for a more equitable distribution of this Income Tax, and will particularly see that those in receipt of large incomes shall pay a much larger percentage than thv.y are going to pay under the present measure.

As
the hon. Speaker ruled the amendment out of order, I feel that it is incumbent UDOn me to say a few words on the third reading of this measure. This Bill introduced by the Finance Minister may be all right as far as it goes; but, coming from the city of Toronto, as he does, I would not expect it to go very far, and my expectation has

been realized. Judging from the views I have heard expressed throughout the country by the man on the street and taking my own personal view, the taxation imposed by this Bill by the Minister of Finance is considered to be a very meagre form of taxation. In this House one question probably has been uppermost in our minds, and that is the question of making the sacrifices of our people, to some extent, a matter of equality, if it is possible to make an equality between sacrifices of men and sacrifices of money. For my own part, and speaking, l think, for every member of this House,
I can say that is an impossibility. But there is this to be said: that a sacrifice in money is a greater sacrifice if a man has to habituate himself to a smaller income than if the law leaves to him a larger income.
I think this Act as presented is not going to satisfy the people at all in regard to comparative sacrifices between the poor and the rich. I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member from St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames), for whom I have the highest regard, and who, I believe, ha6 done an immense service to the country in connection with the Patriotic Fund. In principle, I do not believe the Patriotic Fund should be dependent upon voluntary subscription. I do not believe the soldiers and their dependents should have to rely on what looks like charity. They have done too much for this land and for freedom for us to ask them or their families to be dependent on what looks like charity. I believe that ' is a matter which should have been handled by this Government, and should be paid for by the Canadian people as a part of their taxation. I may say in passing- and I do not want to digress and depart from the rules, but I think it is relevant to the subject-that as far as my country is concerned, it affects the question of taxation generally. My county, Middlesex, part of which I have the honour to represent, has considered that as a cardinal principle, and they have given to the Patriotic Fund $72,000 a year. In addition to that, generous men have contributed in a very liberal manner. The hon. member for St. Antoine (Sir Herbert Ames) said, among other things, that he has heard patriotic rich men say that they did not want any more money when this war was over than they had when it began, or words to that effect. I am the last man in this House to detract from what has been done by the wealthy men of Canada in the way of assistance in this war. I believe their
hearts are in it, just as much as are the hearts of the plain people of this country. But I ask you, Sir, if there is any class of men in this country whose hearts should be more in this war than the wealthy men of this land? They have more to be protected than the poor man. They have more at stake, and if any person or class of persons should be willing to make sacrifices in this war, it is the wealthy men of this land. When patriotic rich men have said that they do not want to be any richer when the war is over than when it began, it is a very-shall I put it mildly?-low idea] of patriotic duty. No man, rich or poor, should want to be as well off when the war is over as when it began. If he is stirred by patriotic emotions, if he has the love of Empire at his heart, and the desire to save the Empire and civilization, he should be willing to be much poorer when this war is over than when it began, if this war means anything to him; for, as .Lloyd George has said, if Germany wins this war, nothing else matters. The member for St. Antoine says that the wealthy man is willing to give of his wealth; that he does not want to be any richer when this war is over than he was when it began. I have read of wealthy men making similar professions; talk is sometimes very cheap. I have read in the public press- and it has not been denied-that one very wealthy man in this country said "To hell with profits."

Order.
Mr. ROSS; That is a quotation; if it is offensive to him, the hon. member for North Grey need not listen to it. It is all very well for wealthy men to make such professions as "to Sheol with profits"-if you like to put it that way. But the man who said that was willing to take $5,000,000 in a year for himself or his company from the poor people of Canada. During this war we want not professions but acts. We should make the wealthy men of this country-in a reasonable, not in a cruel way-pay their share of the burden that is imposed upon us by reason of our participation in this war. Can the sacrifice of the wealthy man who has an income of $100,000-who under the income tax will pay $14,900 and who professes that he is willing to do so-be compared with the sacrifice of the poor widow who, not merely professing that she is willing to sacrifice her three sons on the altar of her country, actually does sacrifice them? There is no comparison at all. The wealthy men of this

country should bear a fair share of the burden of sacrifice made by the Canadian people for the cause of civilization.
The Minister of Finance introduced two measures into this House recently, one of which we discussed to-day. I would characterize the measure now under consideration as the Millionaires' Belief Act. Under this measure the wealthy men will not be asked to make any sacrifices. They are doing nothing to win the war. Whatever they may do from patriotic motives, they are doing nothing under compulsion by this Parliament as a matter of sacrifice. As to the other measure introduced by the Finance Minister, that with relation to the Canadian Northern Bailway system, I would characterize it as The Millionaires' Aid Act -because, to my mind, that is all it is.
The Minister of Finance stated some time ago-although, in the vernacular, he is a little bit wobbly on the subject-that the excess war profits tax would cease to be effective on December 31, 1917. I understand that he intimated in the House this afternoon-I was not here when he did so- that he had changed his mind in so far as profiteering in connection with munitions and war supplies was concerned. I am rattier surprised; nevertheless, I compliment him on his change of heart. As a member of this House, who has the interests of the people at heart-I mean not particularly the people of Toronto, or of the large cities, but the people as a whole- I say emphatically that the Minister of Finance makes a great mistake. When he brought down his Budget he pointed out what he considered to be the many virtues of the excess profits war tax. He pointed out that in the first year of its operation he was getting $12,500,000, and that he would likely get $15,000,000 when the whole returns were in. He said that in the second year he would get $20,000,000, but that he could not . say what he would get in the third year-I do not quarrel with him in that respect, because it would be difficult to calculate the amount that would probably be received. He pointed out what a wonderful law this was; how easily and economically it worked; how everything was simplicity itself in connection with the collection of the tax; how the cost of collection was only one-half of one per cent. Well, the war is still on; the financial necessities of our country are greater than they ever were. The minister deems it necessary to go to the American market to borrow $100,000,000 and to pay thereon almost seven 
per cent interest. Yet, although men are making millions of dollars in the manufacture of munitions and of war supplies, at the expense of the people, my hon. friend says that he will cut off the excess profits tax, so far as it relates to ordinary business profits, at the end of the year 1917. No such action has been taken in England; I submit that this tax should be continued in Canada for the advantage of the people and in order that we may be able to carry on the war to a successful conclusion. Persons who are now subjected to that tax should be required to pay their share. Some of them are making immense profits out of the war, and in view of t-he fact that the end of the war is not yet in sight, there is no reason why they should not continue to pay the tax which has been imposed upon them. It was pointed out this afternoon that a gentleman with highei ideals than some others had turned into the treasury $675,000, an amount which ha considered to be in excess of what he ought to have made. In the light of all these considerations this tax on excess profits should be continued at least until the end of the war, and Parliament should at this session make statutory provision to that effect.
The Government may think that they are following the wishes of the people in passing this very moderate form of taxation. Before this taxation measure was introduced, we had meetings of public bodies all over the country. We had meetings of the labour people, meetings of all the church courts, meetings of the great agricultural classes in the West.
Hear, hear.

Some of my hon. friends are rather sorry for it, I know; they may yet have reason to be more sorry than ever. What has been the general expression of opinion of all these public meetings? They have said: If the Government is going to enforce a compulsory Military Service Act they should just as sedulously enforce compulsory money service upon the people. They have said that in no uncertain tone.
I ask the Prime Minister if the opinions of those people are not to be considered? Is he going to pay no attention to the well-considered opinions of the labouring men of this country? Is he going to pay no attention to the strong opinions expressed by all the religious bodies? Is he going to pay no attention to the opinions of the great agricultural classes as they were recently expressed in the West? Let us take, for instance, my own church-the Scotch

Presbyterian Church in this country. What was the expression of opinion of that body? They said, without any indefinitenese1: If we are going to have compulsory service in regard to man-power, we should have compulsory service in regard to money-power. Does this country consider that the opinion of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Canada, composed of men, some of whom are probably-and I do not wish to say this rudely-the superiors or the equals of men in this House, should not have some attention paid to it? Those men come from all walks of life, from the professional classes, the working classes, the clergy. Their opinion before the people of this country is just as good, just as potent and has just as much right to consideration as the opinion of any hon. member of this House or of any public body in this country. The Scotch people of this country have in this war given of their sons and of their money without stint, and those people convened in their General Assembly have a right to expect from this Government that their opinions, solemnly expressed, shall receive due consideration,.
Under the system of taxation submitted to us in this Bill, every opinion that has been expressed by those bodies, labouring, religious, agricultural, has been entirely disregarded, and we are exacting no sacrifice from the wealthy men of this country. My contention in that regard is stronger when one considers that the Minister of Finance says to this House that, except in regard to the manufacture of munitions, he is going to discontinue the tax which has, for the last two years, been imposed upon this country in regard to excess profits. I know this amendment has been ruled out of order by Your Honour, but I consider it is very unfortunate that, under the rules of the House, you should have that power. I know you have exercised it with absolute impartiality, as you always do. I have no doubt that you may be right in ruling this amendment out of order, but although the Prime Minister has said in *reply to my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), that the consent of the Crown must be obtained for the submission of an amendment calling for an increase of taxation, we know that, as a matter of practice, the recommendation of the Crown means simply the recommendation of the Government, and in this democratic country, we should alter our rules so that any hon. member of this House may be able to submit to the House an amendment for which I believe not only Liberals on this side but
Conservatives on the other side would vote if they had the opportunity.
We are passing through strenuous times, and the end is not yet in sight. We are going to need all our money and all our men in order that victory may be ours. The people of Canada, rich or poor, have but one heart in this issue; they intend to win this war. Generally speaking, they are prepared to pay the price, and this Government, if it were really listening to the voice of the people and not to the voice of just a class of the people, would have submitted a measure of taxation that would receive the fuller approval of the people of Canada than the measure upon which we are passing to-night has received.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Ross) has made a reference to me. Apparently he has not a perfectly clear idea as to the present legislation with regard to the business profits tax Act enacted in 1916. That legislation was enacted in 1916; the tax was payable during that year, in respect of profits made in 1915. It is payable this year in respect of profits made in 1916. It will be payable next year in respect of profits made in 1917.
I am quite clear in regard to that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, if my hon. friend was clear with regard to that, he did not seem to express himself very clearly with Tegard to it, because if that idea is firmly rooted in his mind, I would have expected him to understand that there will be ample opportunity, at the next session, to take any action in respect of the profits that may be made by any company, corporation or individual in this country during the year 1918. We have already provided for taxation of profits made in 1915, 1916 and 1917. That is all dealt with, and the tax in respect of the profits of 1917 will be payable next year.
It will, therefore, be perfectly proper for the Parliament that is to be summoned in the immediate future to make any disposition it may see fit in respect of the profits, if any, that will be earned by any company, corporation, or individual next year.
If my right hon. friend will guarantee to me that he will be Premier of Canada at that time, and that that will be done, I shall be perfectly satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has no faith in his own party.
I do not mean that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend seems to have a great deal of doubt as to what will happen if I am not Premier-
I know what will happen.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
-and I am very much obliged for his expression of confidence as to what will happen if I am Premier.
He has not been very much clearer in his appreciation of what has been said by my hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has explained over and over again that the Business Profits Tax Act enacted in 1916 contained this section as the final clause of the Act:
The provisions of section 3 of this Act shall not continue in force after the 31st day of December, 1917.
I am not aware that any hon. gentleman opposite ha9 raised any question about that particular provision of the Act of 1916. Did my hon. friend raise any protest about it? He did not. It was in the minds of us all at that time that this war might probably reach a triumphant conclusion before the date mentioned in that section, and so the matter passed in that way, except that the Minister of Finance at the present session thought it necessary, in view of the financial situation which has developed through the unexpected length of the war, to increase largely in respect of the business profits earned this year, the taxation that was imposed by the Act of last year. Whenever the question has come up in this House as to the continuation of the business profits tax, the Minister of Finance has made his position perfectly clear. I happen to have under my hand what he said only this afternoon with regard to it, and it shows that the Minister of Finance has made his position perfectly plain. His statement was as follows:
Mr. Pardee:	As I understand this matter,
the hon. Minister of Finance has practically said that the income tax is being introduced in lieu of what is known as the "business profits war tax.
Sir Thomas White:	No, that is not correct.
Mr. Pardee:	As I understand the matter,
the business war tax is to come to an end, and will not be continued after the end of this year.
Sir Thomas White: The business profits war tax, by its terms, comes to an end on December 31st of this year. When that measure was introduced, it was thought the war would be at an end by that time. I stated expressly the other day that we should tax abnormal business profits resulting from the war, and in the next Budget that X bring down we shall deal with that matter.

Mr. Pardee:	Can we take it in this way:
that the present War Tax Profits Bill expires December 31, 1917?
Sir Thomas White. By its terms.
Mr. Pardee:	Will there be a renewal ?
Sir Thomas White:	I have stated that next
year a taxation will he imposed on excess business profits. I stated also the other day that it might he necessary to make some allowance for necessary plant extensions, but I laid down the principle, as strongly as I could, that abnormal business profits due to the war must be abnormally taxed.
The explanation already given, that the tax upon profits during the year 1917 will be exigible during the year 1918 should be entirely satisfactory. So, as my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) has said that he would be perfectly satisfied if an assurance were given to him, and as I adopt the assurance that has already been given by the Minister of Finance, I am confident that the discussion leaves my hon. friend in a perfectly happy, contented and satisfied frame of mind.
The hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) was good enough to indulge in a little chaff towards my colleague the Minister of Finance, with regard to the probability of his presenting a Budget next year. If I should follow his example in that regard I might say that it is very fortunate for my hon. friend from Russell that he presented his criticism of this measure now, as he may never have another opportunity. He was a little in error as to the authority he quoted. It was not Mr. Kuhn, but Mr. Otto H. Kahn, a very well known financial authority in the United States, and a member of the firm of Kahn, Loeb & Company, who has written several treatises with regard to business and taxation.
That is the name I quoted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend called him "Kuhn."
His pronunciation must he bad.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I would call to the attention of the hon. member for Russell and of the hon. member for West Middlesex that when they compare taxation in this country with taxation in the United States they should bear in mind that the business profits tax prevailing in

Canada is very much higher, so I am informed by the Minister of Finance, than any corresponding taxation in the United States at the present time. More than that,
I am ssured by the Minister of Finance, who has made a careful study of the systems of taxation prevailing in the various countries in the world during this war, that the business profits tax of 1916, as 'amended by the Act of 1917, imposes a heavier taxation on profits of that character than is imposed in any other country in the world. So there can be little fault found from the standpoint of my hon. friend or from the standpoint of any one else, with the course which has been pursued by the Minister of Finance in that regard. War-business profits in Canada to-day are paying a heavier tax than similar profits are paying in any other country in the world. So [DOT] much for that.
With regard to the income tax, it is perfectly true that the income tax as recently introduced in the Congress of the United i States is heavier than the income tax proposed here. It was introduced there upon a certain scale, and that scale has been considerably increased. The scale proposed toy the Bill which is now under consideration corresponds approximately, I think, with that which was first introduced in the Congress of the United States. But we shall not have exhausted the legislation that may be possible in this country by the passage of this Bill. The Minister of Finance, in introducing this measure, bad to take into account more than one consideration. In the first place he bad to take this into account; that in so far as this legislation (imposes taxation during the year 1917, it is retroactive in respect of more than half of the year. He had also to take into account what has been put forward very clearly and cogently by the hon. member for St. Antoine, namely that a igreat many persons in this country who are contributing this year as in the past very abundantly and generously from their incomes towards the Canadian Patriotic Fund ought to be considered in that regard. Notwithstanding what has been said by my hon. friend from West Middlesex in depreciation of those people in this country who are blessed with this world's goods, I hold that the vast majority of them are entitled to every commendation for the splendid way in which they have come to the aid of the Canadian Patriotic Fund. Simply because a man may be found here and there
who, although blessed with abundant means, has not done his duty as others have, it is neither fair nor just to oast aspersions upon the community as a whole, because the community as a whole has risen splendidly to the need of the hour.
Would the Prime Minister be good enough to say who in this debate was casting aspersions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross), as I understood him.

I rise to a question of privilege. I think the Prime Minister has entirely misrepresented my remarks, unintentionally, I believe. I commended those wealthy men as a matter of fact. Many of them have done noble things. What I said was that as'a class they should bear their burdens with the poor people of the country, rand I still say so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did not in the least suggest anything to the contrary, but I understood the hon. member for West Middlesex to speak in some such sense as I have mentioned. I am very glad indeed that he did not desire to be understood in that way. On more than one occasion he referred in a somewhat depreciative tone to the people of Toronto, apparently considering, for some reason which I cannot comprehend, that they had failed to do their duty in this regard. I believe the people of Toronto have risen splendidly to the need of the whole country, and have done their full duty in this war in every respect.
The Minister of Finance thought it desirable, for the reasons which have been mentioned, that he should fix the scale of taxation as it is proposed in this Bill. In the first place, he had before him the example of what had been done in the United States. The scale there has since been increased. In the second place, he had before him the fact that this Bill is retroactive for more than one-half of the year 1917. In the third place he had to take into account the fact that those who have contributed so splendidly and generously to the Canadian Patriotic Fund without the expectation that heavy taxation would be imposed upon their incomes, ought to be given for this year the consideration which is rendered by this Bill. All these matters, however, leave it entirely open to the Minister of Finance to take up the question again at the next session and have it dealt with by a Parliament fresh from the

people. There is no doubt that that will be done, so that under the circumstances it seems to me the measure as proposed meets the situation up to the present time. There will be occasion, no doubt, to take it up, for another reason. If we begin taxation upon a heavy scale on incomes in this country, it is hardly within the bounds of probability that the Canadian Patriotic Fund can expect to receive the liberal contributions which have been made to it from private sources in the past, and therefore there may be occasion, on that account, for the Minister of Finance to take the matter up from that point of view, with the intention of making provision for a need which otherwise cannot be met. The hon. member for St. Antoine has, if I remember correctly, spoken of the possible necessity that this may have to be done in another year, and the splendid organization which has been built up by those responsible for the direction and management of the Canadian Patriotic Fund would insure the effective and useful expenditure of any moneys which might be devoted by the Government for that purpose. However, these-are all matters which will have to be considered at some later stage. In the meantime, I venture to submit with a great deal of confidence that the measure proposed by the Minister of Finance is one which meets the situation for the present and will lend itself to such amendment as may be found necessary in the future.

May I ask the Prime Minister a question? As the member for St. Antoine, whom he has quoted, practically said that but a very small proportion of the Patriotic Fund came from the rich man, and the contributions came largely from the poor man, might it not be that this measure of taxation was still taking from the poor man more than he ought to pay, at the same time leaving the rich man practically immune?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not hear the hon. member for St. Antoine make the statement referred to, and I am not aware of the statistics. I would point out to the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) that this measure exempts unmarried persons in respect of an income of $1,500 or less, and it exempts married persons in respect of an income of $3,000 or less. Therefore it does not seem to me it would bear very heavily upon the class of persons he has in mind.
Might I say that the Prime Minister's answer is not a reply to my question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then I did not understand the question.

The member for St. Antoine said that the rich man contributed about one-quarter of the Patriotic Fund, and the rest of the people contributed the balance. My question is this:	Under the
present Bill, if you take the incomes from $6,000 up, which I think will be considered 'by any man in this House as a fair income, irrespective of what may be his circumstances, he may-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentle man is proceeding to make a speech.

I was just going to ask
a question, your Honour. Is it not fair to suppose that under this Bill the poor man is still being mulcted, whilst the man with an income of over $6,000 is being practically left alone?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The terms "rich" and "poor" are relative terms. I do not know what my hon. friend has in mind. I can onljt repeat that no married person will be "mulcted" under this Bill unless he has an income of more than $3,000, and no unmarried person will be "mulcted" under this Bill unless he has an income of at least $1,500. Therefore, it does not appear that the evils my hon. friend has in mind can possibly occur.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill No. 100 respecting Game in the Northwest Territories.-Mr. Roche.-Mr. Rainville in the Chair.
On section 4-Regulations:

Owing to some criticisms
that were offered, we allowed several sections. to stand over for further consideration. The criticisms were made particularly by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) who stated that he would like to see incorporated in the form of a statute what we had proposed to put in the form of regulation. To meet the wishes of the hon. gentleman, and after consideration, we have decided to amend this clause by striking it out and substituting another. I therefore beg to move:
That section 4 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
4. (1) Bxcept as hereinafter provided, the following shall not be hunted, taken, killed,
shot at, wounded, injured or molested in any way during the following times of year respectively :
(a)	Moose, caribou, deer, mountain sheep and mountain goats between the first day of April and the fifteenth day of July, and between the first day of October and the first day of December;
(b)	Minks, fishers and martens between the fifteenth day of March and thel first day of November;
(e)	Otter and beaver between the fifteenth day of May and the first day of October;
(d)	Muskrats between the fifteenth day of May and the first day of October;
(e)	White fox between the first day of April and the fifteenth day of November;
(f)	Partridge, prairie chicken, ptarmigan and other species of grouse between the first day of January and1 the first day of September ;
(g)	Wild geese and wild duck with the exception of eider duck between the fifteenth day of December and the first day of September.
(2)	Except as hereinafter provided, no eggs in the nest of any of the said birds or in the nest of any other species of wild fowl, shall be taken, destroyed, injured or molested at any time of the year.
(3)	Notwithstanding anything contained in subsections 1 and 2 the game therein mentioned may be lawfully hunted, taken or killed and the eggs of birds therein mentioned may be lawfully taken by Indians or Eskimos who are bona fide inhabitants of the Northwest Territories or by other bona fide inhabitants of the said territories and by explorers or surveyors who are engaged in any exploration, survey or other examination of the country, but only when such persons are actually in need of such game or eggs to prevent starvation.
(4)	Except as hereinafter provided, buffalo or bison shall not be hunted, taken, killed, shot at, wounded, injured or molested at any time of the year.
(5)	Except as hereinafter provided, musk-ox and wapiti or elk shall not be hunted, taken, killed, shot at, wounded, injured or molested at any time of the year except in such zones and during such period as the Governor in Council may prescribe.
(6)	Except as hereinafter provided, white pelicans shall not be hunted, taken, killed, shot at. wounded, injured or molested at any time of the year.
(7)	Except as hereinafter provided, the following shall not be hunted, taken, killed, shot at, wounded, injured or molested in any way.
Subclause (a) of Clause 6 of Section 4 :
(a) Wild swan, until the first day of January, 1928.
(b) Eider duck, until the first day of January, 1923.
(8)	Notwithstanding the provisions of subsections 1, 3, 4, 5 and 6, the minister or any officer or person authorized by him, may issue a permit to any person to take or kill at any time such mammals and birds or take the eggs or nests of birds, for scientific or propagation purposes.
(9)	Excepting a native-born Indian, Eskimo or halfbreed who is a bona fide resident of the Northwest Territories no person shall engage in hunting, trapping or trading or trafficking



in game without first securing a license so to do.
(a)	The fees for such licenses when issued to a bona fide resident of the Northwest Territories shall he:
For hunting and trapping, $2.
For trading or trafficking, $5.
(b)	The fees for such licenses when issued to non-residents of the Northwest Territories shall be fixed by the Governor in Council.
(10)	The Governor in Council may make regulations:
(a)	Regulating or prohibiting the use or
possession of poison, ammunition, explosives, traps, snares, spring-guns, firearms and other implements, appliances and contrivances for hunting, killing, taking, trapping, destroying or capturing game:	Provided that such prohibition shall not apply to such types of guns, rifles, traps and ammunition as are now in common use;
(b)	permitting the hunting, killing, taking, capturing or trapping of specimens of game for scientific or propagation purposes;
(c)	governing the issue of licenses and permits and prescribing the terms and conditions thereof;
(d)	authorizing the appointment by the minister of game officers and game wardens and prescribing their duties;
(e)	regulating the possession of and transportation of game;
(f)	for any other purposes which may be deemed expedient for carrying out the provisions and intentions of this Act whether such regulations are of the kind enumerated or not.
(11)	Any regulation made under the provisions of this section may be made to apply to the whole or any part of the Northwest Territories.
For caribou, deer, mountain sheep, etc., we are making the dates much the same as they now are in the Northwest Territories Game Act, with such slight changes as are necessitated by the migratory bird treaty which has been entered into between the United States and Canada and which has been confirmed by this Parliament. These amendments have been submitted to my hon. friend from Edmonton and I may say he approves of them.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 7-Game officers to be justices of the peace:

Every game officer under the authority of this Act and of the regulations was to be an ex-officio justice of the peace for the Northwest Territories. We are striking out this section, and, therefore, I move section 7 be struck out. Amendment agreed to.
On section 8-Game officers may appoint constables:

In view of the elimination of section 7, it is necessary to change section 8, which, in its original form, provided for 
a person being brought to trial before a game officer. I therefore move:
That subsection 2 of section 8 be amended by striking out the words "or game officer" In the third line thereof.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 10-Seizure:

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 17-Separate offences:
Mr. RO'C'HE:	A person might consider
it desirable and profitable to take chances of offending on a large scale, if the killing, trapping, taking or capturing of each animal did not constitute a separate offence, and that was the reason this section was inserted. When this measure was before the House on a former occasion objection was taken to the words in this section " or having in his possession," and we are eliminating those words, and confining it to the killing, trapping, taking, or capturing. The section as amended will read as follows:
The killing, taking, trapping or capturing of each animal or bird contrary to the provisions of this Act or a regulation shall constitute a separate offence.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 19-Penalties:

The maximum penalty for killing such animals as the musk-ox and buffalo, is made $600 and the minimum penalty $5 for other offences. The section, as amended, reads as follows:
Any person who violates any of the provisions of this Act for which no other penalty is provided, or of any regulation, shall be guilty of an offence andl shall be liable on summary conviction to-
(a)	A fine not exceeding $500 or less than $100 or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding six months or to both fine and imprisonment for any offence against subsections 4 and 5 of section 4.
(b)	A fine not exceeding $200 or less than $50 or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding three months or to both fine and imprisonment for any offence under subsection 9 of seotion 4.
(c)	A fine not exceeding $100 or less than $5 or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding two months or to both fine and imprisonment for any other offence against this Act or a regulation.
On section 18:

This is a new section. I move that the following section be added to the Bill, as section 18:
18. (1) Whenever by this Act it is made an offence to do any act without holding a license therefor, the onus In any prosecution shall be upon the person charged, to prove that ha was the holder of the license required by this Act.
(2) In any prosecution under this Act the onus of proof as to his bona fide residence in the Northwest Territories shall be upon the defendant.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 22-Commencement of Act:
I move that this section be struck out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to.
Bill reported as amended and amendments concurred in.
On motion of Mr. Roche for the third reading of the Bill:

As the amendments have been run through somewhat hurriedly, I would bespeak of the minister a very careful comparison of the typewritten copies placed before the committee, and if there are found to be any differences the Bill could be referred back for correction.
Yes.	*
